title: After the LG's Remarks on Great Nicobar, Several Questions Remain
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Following the LG's remarks on Great Nicobar, questions remain on transparency, consultation and public accountability.
html:
Recent remarks by the Lieutenant Governor defending the Great Nicobar Project have reignited debate over one of the most ambitious development initiatives proposed for the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

In the interview, the LG strongly rejected claims that indigenous communities would be harmed by the project and described opposition to the initiative as part of a sustained campaign aimed at delaying or obstructing development. He also emphasized that the project had undergone multiple stages of scrutiny, including environmental clearances and legal review.

Those statements provide the administration's perspective.

However, they also raise several broader questions that continue to be discussed by citizens, researchers, environmental groups and public policy observers.

Media Accessibility

After nearly a decade in office, has the administration provided sufficient opportunities for open press conferences, unscripted media interactions and direct questioning by journalists?

Transparency and Public Communication

Why are major projects often explained in detail after public controversy emerges rather than through proactive engagement from the beginning?

Could earlier and more frequent communication have reduced misunderstanding and mistrust?

Environmental Concerns

The administration maintains that environmental safeguards are in place and that legal clearances have been obtained.

Yet, have all concerns raised by environmental experts been fully addressed, or do some issues still require continued public scrutiny and independent monitoring?

Public Consultation

To what extent were local communities, researchers, environmental specialists and elected representatives involved during the planning and approval stages?

Were consultation processes broad enough to ensure that diverse viewpoints were heard?

Access to Information

Are environmental assessments, monitoring reports, compliance reports and project progress updates easily accessible to ordinary citizens?

If not, should greater public disclosure become standard practice?

Democratic Accountability

As a Union Territory without a legislative assembly, what mechanisms exist to ensure effective public oversight of major policy and development decisions?

Are existing institutions sufficient to provide accountability and transparency?

Measuring Development Outcomes

Beyond major announcements and infrastructure proposals, what measurable improvements have occurred over the past decade in:

  • Healthcare
  • Education
  • Employment opportunities
  • Transportation
  • Inter-island connectivity
  • Public services

How should these outcomes be evaluated and communicated to the public?

Administrative Responsiveness

How effectively has the administration responded to local grievances, infrastructure challenges and long-standing public concerns?

Do citizens feel they have adequate channels through which their concerns can be heard and addressed?

The Larger Question

The Great Nicobar debate is ultimately about more than a single project.

It reflects a broader discussion about development, environmental stewardship, public participation and governance.

The administration has presented its position clearly.

The public, however, may continue to ask whether transparency, engagement and accountability have kept pace with the scale of decisions being made.

Constructive debate is a normal feature of democracy, and difficult questions often remain even after official explanations have been provided.

title: Dr. Arun K. Mallik Outlines AAP Roadmap for Andaman & Nicobar, Says Health, Education and Local Issues Will Be Priorities
author: Dweep Tulika
description: AAP Andaman President Dr Arun K. Mallik outlines his priorities on health, education, jobs, water, electricity and public grievances.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | August 12, 2026

Newly appointed Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) Andaman & Nicobar State President Dr. Arun K. Mallik addressed the media in Sri Vijaya Puram on Wednesday, outlining his political approach, priorities and proposed roadmap for addressing issues affecting the Islands.

The press briefing was Dr. Mallik's first major media interaction following his appointment as the party's State President.

Thanks AAP leadership for trust

Dr. Mallik began by thanking AAP national leadership for entrusting him with the responsibility. He expressed gratitude to AAP National Convenor Arvind Kejriwal, Rajya Sabha MP and senior AAP leader Sanjay Singh, AAP's Andaman & Nicobar in-charge Adv. Somnath Bharti, and other senior leaders and party workers.

He said the appointment was an important moment for him and acknowledged the support of people associated with the party during the process leading to his appointment.

Dr. Mallik said he had been interested in reviving AAP's organisational presence in the Islands for several years and stated that he had written to the party's national leadership in 2022 expressing his desire to work towards reviving the party in Andaman & Nicobar.

Health and education among major priorities

Outlining the party's proposed priorities, Dr. Mallik said health and education would receive particular attention, while acknowledging that challenges exist across almost every sector in the Islands.

He also referred to issues concerning employment, roads, shipping, transportation, electricity and water supply.

He described AAP's approach as "alternative politics", saying the party intended to work with the local Administration to pursue solutions to problems faced by ordinary citizens rather than focusing only on protests.

100% job reservation and Ladakh model

Employment for Islanders emerged as another major issue in Dr. Mallik's address.

He supported the demand for 100% job reservation for Islanders, referring to concerns over employment opportunities for local residents. He said the party would seek to raise the issue with the Islands' MPs and senior political leaders and take it up at the Centre.

He also referred to the Ladakh model as something he believed could be examined for implementation in Andaman & Nicobar.

Water, electricity, roads and shipping

Dr. Mallik identified water supply and electricity as long-standing issues in the Islands. He said these were chronic problems that could not necessarily be resolved through a single protest or immediate intervention.

He estimated that addressing such infrastructure issues comprehensively could require a sustained effort over a period of years.

He also criticised what he described as gaps between government plans and their implementation at the local level, citing the condition and execution of the NH-4 road project as an example.

Dweep Tulika asks three questions

During the question-and-answer session, Dweep Tulika News Editor-in-Chief Mr. R. Vineeth asked Dr. Mallik three questions concerning the party's identity, neglected public concerns and his first priority as State President.

1. What differentiates AAP from other political parties in the Islands?

Asked to identify the difference in one word, Dr. Mallik described AAP's approach as:

"Alternative politics."

He explained that the party's focus was on issues affecting ordinary people and said it intended to work with citizens and the local Administration to understand and resolve their problems.

2. What public concern is being neglected?

In response to the second question, Dr. Mallik said he believed people were facing difficulties across different sectors.

He particularly discussed healthcare, arguing that public information about available healthcare facilities was not reaching people adequately. He cited the Sub-District Hospital at Diglipur and said that, in his assessment, it had specialist doctors and available medicines, although shortages and deficiencies remained.

He also identified water and electricity as continuing public concerns, describing them as chronic issues. He said education was another important area requiring attention.

3. What will be his first priority as AAP President?

Asked what he would take up first as the newly appointed State President, Dr. Mallik said his immediate priority would be day-to-day issues and injustices affecting ordinary people.

He said he had already been communicating with government officials and taking up issues with the Administration. He cited matters including alleged illegal construction and other complaints where he said he would seek evidence and raise the issues with the concerned authorities.

He also highlighted healthcare-related emergencies as an area of concern.

Referring to a recent incident involving the deaths of two patients after a ship had departed, Dr. Mallik questioned whether adequate medical and emergency arrangements were available during such transportation. He said he had taken up the matter with the Health Department and called for an appropriate protocol for emergency patient transfers.

He further argued that vessels equipped for healthcare-related services should be appropriately deployed when required and that patients being transferred by ship should have appropriate medical support on board.

"Doctor Mallik will do what is right"

Towards the conclusion of the briefing, Dr. Mallik said his approach would be to take up issues that he believes are in the interest of ordinary Islanders, irrespective of which political party is involved.

He said the party would continue engaging with the Administration and raising issues concerning public welfare.

The briefing therefore provided an early indication of the priorities Dr. Mallik intends to pursue as the newly appointed AAP State President, with healthcare, education, employment, water, electricity, transportation, infrastructure and day-to-day public grievances featuring prominently in his address.

title: US Vice President JD Vance Arrives in Switzerland for Iran Nuclear Talks
author: Dweep Tulika
description: US Vice President JD Vance has arrived in Switzerland for talks with Iran on nuclear issues and regional stability.
html:
US Vice President JD Vance has arrived in Switzerland for high-level talks with Iran focused on nuclear issues, regional security and diplomatic engagement.

Geneva, June 21:

US Vice President JD Vance arrived in Switzerland on Sunday to participate in high-level discussions with Iranian representatives aimed at addressing concerns surrounding Tehran's nuclear programme and reducing tensions in the Middle East.

The negotiations are being held at the Burgenstock resort near Lucerne and are expected to continue over the coming days.

The talks represent a significant diplomatic effort by both sides amid ongoing concerns regarding regional stability, security and the future of nuclear-related agreements.

Officials from the United States and Iran are expected to discuss a range of issues, including Iran's nuclear activities, regional security challenges and measures to support a recently announced ceasefire arrangement.

Prior to his departure for Switzerland, Vice President Vance expressed optimism that the discussions could help advance diplomatic engagement and contribute to peace and stability in the region.

Iranian representatives, including senior government officials, have also arrived in Switzerland to participate in the negotiations.

The talks come at a time of heightened international concern regarding conflicts in the Middle East and the security of critical maritime trade routes in the region.

Observers believe the outcome of the discussions could influence future relations between Washington and Tehran while also affecting broader geopolitical dynamics across the Middle East.

The international community is closely monitoring the negotiations, with hopes that diplomatic engagement may help reduce tensions and encourage long-term regional stability.

title: Former NCERT Director Defends Academic Autonomy of NCERT Amid Textbook Debate
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Former NCERT Director J S Rajput defended NCERT’s academic autonomy amid debates over textbook content and curriculum.
html:
New Delhi, 25 February 2026:

Former National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) Director J S Rajput has stated that the Supreme Court of India has its “limitations” and should respect the academic decisions taken by NCERT.

Speaking amid ongoing discussions surrounding NCERT textbooks and curriculum matters, Rajput emphasized that the institution plays an important role in shaping the nation’s future. He noted that generations of leaders, professionals, and public figures have studied through NCERT educational materials.

Rajput argued that while the judiciary deserves respect, educational institutions should also be trusted in matters related to academic expertise and curriculum development.

Referring to traditional values, he highlighted the importance of respecting teachers and educational bodies, stating that institutions involved in nation-building should be allowed to function independently within their domain.

He further remarked that instead of questioning NCERT’s role, institutions should focus on improving their own systems and functioning. According to him, the council’s decisions are guided by academic considerations and long-term educational objectives.

Addressing criticism over textbook content, Rajput said that NCERT has not attempted to undermine any institution and that educational material should be evaluated over time through feedback from students and educators.

The remarks come amid wider national discussions regarding curriculum development, educational reforms, and the role of institutions in shaping public discourse.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume VIII, Issue No. 12, dated 20 March 2026.

title: Vakkom Purushothaman: The Lieutenant Governor Who Stayed Close to the Islanders
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Remembering Vakkom B. Purushothaman's 1993–1996 tenure as Lieutenant Governor of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | August 24, 2026

When people in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands remember Vakkom B. Purushothaman, they remember a former Lieutenant Governor whose tenure was closely associated with public administration and engagement with the Islanders.

Purushothaman served as the 6th Lieutenant Governor of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands from March 19, 1993, to March 18, 1996. Government records from the period document him functioning as Lieutenant Governor and Administrator of the Union Territory.

A Three-Year Tenure in the Islands

Purushothaman arrived in the Islands after a long political and administrative career in Kerala and Parliament. His tenure in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands came at a time when the Union Territory was dealing with the challenges of administering a geographically dispersed population spread across numerous islands.

During his tenure, official records show his involvement in matters concerning local governance, Panchayati Raj and administration.

In 1994, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands introduced the Panchayats Regulation, 1994, providing a framework for local self-government. During 1995, several notifications were issued under the new framework by Purushothaman in his capacity as Lieutenant Governor (Administrator). These included the constitution of Panchayat Samitis across areas including Diglipur, Mayabunder, Rangat, Ferrargunj, Port Blair, Little Andaman and Campbell Bay.

Other official notifications from March 1995 also show the administration under his tenure constituting Gram Sabhas across villages under the Panchayats framework.

A Governor Who Was Remembered for Public Contact

Accounts published after his death describe Purushothaman as an administrator who maintained a close connection with ordinary residents during his time in the Islands.

One retrospective account recalled that he regularly walked around Port Blair and interacted with residents, listening to their complaints and concerns. It also described his tenure as one in which he took a strong interest in the development of the Islands. These are retrospective accounts rather than official administrative records, and are therefore best understood as recollections of his time in office.

The former Lieutenant Governor was also remembered by the Andaman and Nicobar Administration after his death in 2023. In its condolence message, the then Lieutenant Governor described Purushothaman as an able administrator and reformer committed to the welfare, growth and progress of the Islands, and said Islanders would remember his affection for them.

An Administrator Associated With Development

Retrospective assessments of Purushothaman's career have also credited his tenure in the Islands with strengthening the Union Territory's development and tourism profile.

A later account described his tenure as Lieutenant Governor as a period in which he helped place the Islands more firmly on the tourism map.

However, individual claims about specific projects, inspections or decisions during his tenure require separate documentary verification and should not automatically be attributed to him without supporting records.

Beyond Andaman and Nicobar

Purushothaman's public career continued long after he left the Islands.

He subsequently served as Governor of Mizoram from 2011 to 2014 and briefly as Governor of Tripura in 2014. Earlier, he had served as a Member of Parliament, Kerala minister and Speaker of the Kerala Legislative Assembly.

He died on July 31, 2023, aged 95.

Remembering the “Island” Chapter

For the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, however, his three-year tenure remains a distinct chapter in his long public career.

His period as Lieutenant Governor coincided with important developments in the Union Territory's local-governance framework, including the implementation of the 1994 Panchayats Regulation and the subsequent constitution of Panchayat institutions across different parts of the Islands.

The available records, together with later recollections from people familiar with his tenure, present a picture of an administrator whose time in the Islands combined governance, institutional development and public engagement.

For Islanders who remember that period, Vakkom Purushothaman's name remains connected not merely to the office he held, but to the relationship he was remembered as having built with the people of the Islands.

Dweep Tulika | A Truthful & Unbiased Perspective

title: TSG Bhasker Intervenes After Police Recruitment Aspirants Denied Stadium Access
author: Dweep Tulika
description: TSG Bhasker met sports officials after police recruitment aspirants were denied access to Netaji Stadium due to Independence Day preparations.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram, August 01: 

Hundreds of youths preparing for the upcoming police recruitment physical examination faced inconvenience after Netaji Stadium was closed for 15 days in connection with preparations for the Independence Day celebrations.

According to information received, the stadium is usually closed for around five days each year during Independence Day preparations. This year's extended closure affected the regular practice sessions of many police recruitment aspirants who rely on the stadium for their physical training.

Following representations from the affected candidates, Shri TSG Bhasker, Chairman of the Campaign Committee of the Andaman & Nicobar Territorial Congress Committee (ANTCC), visited Netaji Stadium and interacted with the aspirants to understand their concerns.

He subsequently met Shri Ranjit Kumar, Assistant Director (Sports), and requested that suitable alternative arrangements be made to ensure that the candidates' preparation for the physical examination was not disrupted.

Responding to the request, Shri Ranjit Kumar agreed to provide an alternative practice venue, enabling the aspirants to continue their training during the temporary closure of the stadium.

Shri TSG Bhasker expressed appreciation to the Assistant Director (Sports) for responding promptly to the concerns raised by the candidates.

The alternative arrangement is expected to help police recruitment aspirants continue their physical preparation without interruption until Netaji Stadium reopens after the Independence Day preparations.

title: Power Cuts Force Islanders to Pay for Their Own Backup
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Frequent power cuts in Andaman and Nicobar are forcing residents and businesses to rely on inverters and batteries amid questions over reliable electr
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | August 23, 2026

Frequent and prolonged power interruptions across parts of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are increasingly affecting everyday life, with residents not only losing hours of electricity but also being forced to spend their own money on inverters, batteries and other backup arrangements to maintain basic household and business activities.

For many families, an inverter has gradually shifted from an optional convenience to an essential household expense. During repeated outages, residents depend on backup power for fans, lights, internet routers, computers and other basic electrical equipment. Small businesses face similar pressures, while students struggle to study during interruptions.

The burden becomes particularly difficult in the Islands' hot and humid climate. A prolonged outage can mean several hours without fans or cooling, while households dependent on electric pumps, refrigerators and other appliances face additional difficulties.

The problem is not confined to Sri Vijaya Puram. Reports from Long Island and Diglipur have highlighted serious generation constraints and dependence on diesel generator sets. In Long Island, concerns have been raised over the functioning of its diesel generator capacity, while Diglipur has also faced recurring power-supply problems.

From Election Promise to Ground Reality

The electricity situation also raises questions about commitments made during the 2024 Lok Sabha election.

The BJP's local Sankalp Patra for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands promised round-the-clock clean water and electricity to every household, irrespective of remoteness.

Bishnu Pada Ray, the BJP candidate at the time, subsequently won the lone Lok Sabha seat and became the Islands' Member of Parliament.

Yet recurring power interruptions remain a concern in several parts of the Islands.

This does not necessarily mean that no action has been taken. The Administration and Electricity Department have pursued additional generation capacity and longer-term projects. A proposed 50-MW LNG-based power project at Hope Town is intended to strengthen the Islands' power supply, while other generation and distribution measures have also been undertaken.

However, the key question for residents is increasingly simple: When will reliable electricity become a reality in their homes, rather than something they have to compensate for with their own money?

The Electricity Department itself acknowledges the unique challenge posed by the Islands' geography. Unlike mainland areas connected through a large integrated grid, the electrified islands operate through separate power systems, with individual powerhouses catering to local areas.

That geographical challenge is real, but residents say it cannot become a permanent explanation for unreliable service.

For a family buying an inverter, installing a battery and continuing to pay its electricity bill, the issue is no longer merely about an occasional outage. It is about paying twice — once for electricity service and again for protection against its interruption.

With the 2024 election promise of round-the-clock electricity still fresh in public memory, residents now have a legitimate question:

What concrete measures have been completed, what remains pending, and when can Islanders expect dependable power without having to maintain their own backup systems?

Dweep Tulika | A Truthful & Unbiased Perspective

title: AN-32 Crash Rekindles Debate on Ageing Military Aircraft: Is It Time for India to Accelerate Fleet Modernisation?
author: Dweep Tulika
description: The recent AN-32 crash has renewed debate over ageing military aircraft, fleet modernisation and defence preparedness.
html:
By Dweep Tulika Defence Desk

The recent crash of an Indian Air Force (IAF) AN-32 transport aircraft near Jorhat in Assam has once again brought the spotlight onto one of the Air Force's oldest and most trusted workhorses. The accident claimed the lives of five Air Warriors while one crew member survived, prompting the IAF to order a Court of Inquiry into the incident.

While the cause of the crash remains under investigation, the tragedy has reignited a broader national debate: How long should military aircraft remain in service, and is India investing enough in replacing ageing platforms?

The Backbone of Tactical Airlift

The Antonov AN-32 was inducted into the Indian Air Force in 1984. Designed for operations in hot and high-altitude environments, the Soviet-origin aircraft became the backbone of India's tactical airlift capability.

For more than four decades, the aircraft has transported troops, ammunition, relief supplies, and equipment across some of the most challenging terrains in the world, including Ladakh, Arunachal Pradesh, Siachen Glacier, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

India remains the world's largest operator of the AN-32 fleet. The aircraft delivered to India were factory-new and entered service between 1984 and 1991, making the oldest surviving airframes approximately 42 years old today.

Does Age Alone Cause Aircraft Crashes?

A common perception is that old aircraft are inherently unsafe. Aviation experts, however, caution against such assumptions.

Aircraft are retired not according to age alone but based on structural fatigue, flying hours, maintenance history, and airworthiness certification.

Over the years, the AN-32 fleet has undergone extensive overhauls, avionics upgrades, structural inspections, and life-extension programmes. Many critical components are routinely replaced during scheduled maintenance cycles.

Experts note that a well-maintained aircraft can remain operational for decades. Several military aircraft worldwide have safely exceeded 50 years of service through modernization and rigorous inspections.

Nevertheless, ageing airframes bring challenges such as fatigue monitoring, corrosion management, spare-parts availability, and increasing maintenance costs.

A History of AN-32 Accidents

The AN-32 has suffered several major accidents during its service with the IAF.

Among the most notable were:

  • 2009: Crash in Arunachal Pradesh killing 13 personnel.

  • 2016: Bay of Bengal disappearance during a Chennai-Port Blair flight, killing all 29 onboard.

  • 2019: Crash in Arunachal Pradesh after departing Jorhat, killing 13 personnel.

  • 2026: Jorhat crash claiming five lives.

Investigations into previous accidents revealed varied causes ranging from navigational errors in adverse weather to controlled flight into terrain. Importantly, no major AN-32 crash has officially been attributed solely to the aircraft's age.

Lessons from Global Aviation

History shows that aircraft age can contribute to accidents, but rarely acts alone.

Several famous international aviation disasters involved ageing aircraft where structural fatigue, improper repairs, or cumulative wear played a significant role. These cases demonstrated that maintenance quality and inspection standards are often more important than the aircraft's calendar age.

Many countries continue operating aircraft older than India's AN-32 fleet. The United States Air Force flies B-52 bombers that are more than 60 years old, while numerous air forces continue operating C-130 transport aircraft that have served for over five decades.

The key difference lies in continuous modernization and structural life-extension programmes.

The MiG-21 Comparison

Within India, the aircraft most frequently associated with ageing concerns was the MiG-21.

The fighter remained in service for nearly six decades before its retirement. During that period, it accumulated hundreds of accidents and became a symbol of India's struggle to replace legacy platforms on schedule.

Defence analysts often point out that the issue was not simply the aircraft's age but the combination of prolonged service, delayed replacement programmes, maintenance challenges, and evolving operational requirements.

The AN-32 fleet now finds itself at a similar crossroads.

Defence Budget and Modernisation

India currently ranks among the world's top military spenders. However, experts argue that the challenge is not merely the size of the defence budget but how it is allocated.

A substantial portion of defence expenditure is consumed by salaries, pensions, and operational costs. Consequently, funds available for modernization and new acquisitions remain limited compared to India's growing strategic requirements.

India faces simultaneous challenges along the China border, the Pakistan frontier, the Indian Ocean Region, and its island territories. Maintaining readiness across these fronts requires continuous investment in transport aircraft, fighters, drones, air defence systems, and naval assets.

The Road Ahead

The AN-32 has served India with distinction for over four decades and remains one of the most important aircraft in the IAF inventory. However, as the fleet ages, questions regarding replacement timelines and modernization priorities will only grow louder.

The ongoing Court of Inquiry into the Jorhat crash will determine whether the accident resulted from technical failure, maintenance issues, weather conditions, human factors, or other operational circumstances.

Until then, attributing the tragedy solely to aircraft age would be premature.

What remains certain is that the crash has once again highlighted a challenge faced by militaries across the world: balancing operational necessity with the demands of modernization.

For India, the debate surrounding the AN-32 is no longer just about one aircraft. It is about the future direction of military preparedness in an increasingly complex security environment.

title: When Public Space Becomes a Question of Livelihood: The Street Vendor Dilemma in Sri Vijaya Puram
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Sri Vijaya Puram faces a difficult balance between clearing encroachments, protecting public spaces and safeguarding street vendors' livelihoods.
html:
By Dweep Tulika

There is an uncomfortable question emerging on the streets of Sri Vijaya Puram:

When the administration removes a roadside vendor in the name of clearing public space, where does the protection of that vendor's livelihood begin and end?

The question is not whether roads, footpaths and public land should remain accessible. They should.

Illegal occupation of government land and obstruction of pedestrian movement cannot simply be ignored.

But a street vendor is not automatically the same thing as an encroacher.

That distinction is particularly important because street vending in India is governed by a specific legal framework — the Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014 — and Sri Vijaya Puram Municipal Council itself lists the Act, the Union Territory's 2015 Rules and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands Street Vendors Scheme, 2016 among the regulations applicable to the municipality.

Clearing Encroachments Is One Thing. Removing Livelihoods Is Another.

In April 2026, the District Administration, in coordination with SVPMC, conducted an eviction drive around Corbyn's Cove Junction and towards Corbyn's Cove beach.

According to the Administration's account, 16 unauthorised structures, including makeshift stalls and temporary shops, were removed from Government Revenue land. Four additional encroachments were removed in the Corbyn's Cove area, and approximately 600 square metres of government land was reclaimed.

The Administration said the structures were operating without valid permission and were affecting pedestrian movement and public access.

If those structures were genuinely unauthorised occupations of government land, removing them is within the government's responsibility.

But that action should not automatically become a justification for treating every small vendor as an encroacher.

A person selling vegetables from a cart, running a small food stall or selling locally produced goods operates within a very different legal and economic reality from someone who has permanently occupied government land without permission.

The law recognises that difference.

The Law Does Not Simply Say: Remove the Vendor

The 2014 Street Vendors Act establishes a system through which street vendors are surveyed, identified and issued Certificates of Vending (CoV) by the Town Vending Committee.

It also provides for vending zones and establishes a framework for regulating vending rather than simply eliminating it.

Importantly, where the number of eligible vendors exceeds the capacity of a particular vending zone, the law provides a prescribed mechanism for accommodating remaining vendors in an adjoining vending zone, where possible avoiding unnecessary relocation.

That changes the nature of the debate.

The question should not merely be:

“Is this vendor occupying public space?”

It should also be:

“Is this a legally recognised vendor, and if the existing location is unsuitable, what lawful alternative has been provided?”

SVPMC Appears to Recognise the Need for Regulation Rather Than Elimination

There is an important development that deserves attention.

In June 2026, SVPMC announced a ward-wise survey of street vendors, conducted through the Town Vending Committee under the 2014 Act. The survey ran from July 6 to August 1 and was intended to establish the genuineness of street vendors and facilitate the issuance of Certificates of Vending to eligible vendors.

Vendors were instructed to be physically present with their carts during the survey and provide identification and other required information.

That is significant.

It suggests that the municipality is not merely trying to remove street vending. It is attempting to identify, regulate and formally recognise eligible vendors.

The challenge, therefore, is ensuring that enforcement and recognition do not work against each other.

A Vendor Cannot Be Told to Become Legal and Simultaneously Lose the Opportunity to Become Legal

Imagine a small vendor who has depended on a particular location for years.

The municipality says:

“You need a Certificate of Vending.”

The vendor says:

“I am ready to register.”

The survey is conducted.

But before the vendor receives formal recognition, the vending location is cleared.

That creates a legitimate question:

How is the transition supposed to work?

The answer cannot simply be that vendors should move somewhere else.

A vending zone must be practical enough for a livelihood to survive.

A location where there are no customers may technically provide space but economically destroy the business.

This is particularly important for vendors selling perishable goods such as vegetables, fruits, milk products and prepared food.

For such vendors, location is not merely a convenience.

It is part of their livelihood.

There Is Already an Example of an Alternative Approach

In March 2026, SVPMC announced that it had developed a dedicated open market space at Junglighat for vendors who traditionally conduct Sunday vending activities.

The council described the space as an organised open market and encouraged local vendors to use it subject to applicable norms.

That is potentially the better model.

Instead of only asking:

“How do we remove vendors from here?”

the administration can ask:

“How do we organise vending so that roads and footpaths remain accessible while vendors can continue earning?”

That is the balance the law is designed to facilitate.

Public Convenience Matters — But So Does Economic Dignity

Nobody wants congested roads.

Nobody wants pedestrians forced onto busy streets because stalls have occupied footpaths.

Nobody wants government land to be permanently taken over by unauthorised structures.

But there is another reality that cannot be ignored.

For many small vendors, the cart or stall is not a side business. It is the business.

The person standing behind that cart may not have a shop, commercial property or substantial capital.

The difference between having a place to sell and having nowhere to sell can mean the difference between earning an income and earning nothing.

Urban management therefore has to be more sophisticated than simply clearing whatever looks untidy.

A city can be clean without becoming hostile to small livelihoods.

A footpath can remain accessible without eliminating every vendor.

A vending zone can be regulated without turning it into a punishment zone.

And enforcement can be firm without being economically blind.

The Questions SVPMC Should Answer

The ongoing process raises several legitimate public questions:

  • How many street vendors have been identified within SVPMC's jurisdiction?
  • How many currently possess valid Certificates of Vending?
  • How many vendors have been removed from their previous locations?
  • How many have been given alternative vending spaces?
  • Which areas have been formally designated as vending zones?
  • Which areas have been declared no-vending zones, and on whose recommendation?
  • How many vendors have been relocated rather than simply evicted?
  • What happens to vendors who were present for years but were not included in the latest survey?
  • Are the same principles of public-space enforcement being applied consistently to large and small commercial interests?

These are not unreasonable questions.

They are questions of transparency.

The Real Issue Is Not “Vendors Versus Government”

It is tempting to frame the story as a confrontation between street vendors and the municipality.

That would be too simplistic.

The municipality has a legitimate responsibility to maintain public roads, footpaths, sanitation, traffic movement and public land.

At the same time, the government has created a legal framework specifically recognising street vending as a livelihood that requires protection and regulation.

Therefore, the real issue is how the two responsibilities are reconciled.

If a structure is an illegal occupation of government land, remove it.

If a vendor is obstructing a road or footpath, regulate the location.

If a vending zone has reached capacity, follow the prescribed mechanism.

If a vendor qualifies under the law, provide the appropriate certificate.

And if relocation is necessary, provide a genuine alternative rather than merely telling a person to disappear from one street.

A Cleaner City Should Not Have to Mean an Emptier Livelihood

Sri Vijaya Puram has every right to demand orderly streets.

Its residents have every right to walk safely on footpaths.

The Administration has every right to protect government land.

But small vendors also have a right to expect that the law will distinguish between illegal occupation and regulated livelihood.

The success of municipal governance should not be measured only by how many stalls disappear after an eviction drive.

It should also be measured by whether the city can organise its public spaces without unnecessarily destroying the livelihoods of the people who depend on them.

The objective should not be a city with no vendors.

Nor should it be a city where public spaces are allowed to become chaotic.

The objective should be something more difficult — and more responsible:

A city where public space is protected, vending is regulated, and a poor person's livelihood is not treated as an encroachment merely because the person does not own a shop.

That is the balance Sri Vijaya Puram now has an opportunity to demonstrate.

Dweep Tulika | A Truthful & Unbiased Perspective

title: Adani Wins All Eight Long-Term Coal Power Tenders in BJP-Ruled States: Report
author: Dweep Tulika
description: A Reporters' Collective investigation claims Adani Group won all eight long-term coal power tenders floated by BJP-ruled states.
html:
Delhi, June 20:
A recent investigation by The Reporters' Collective has claimed that the Adani Group won all eight long-term coal power tenders floated by BJP-ruled states between 2024 and early 2026.
According to the report, the projects could generate an estimated revenue of approximately ₹13.27 lakh crore over their operational lifetime, with most power purchase agreements extending for nearly 25 years.

The investigation examined power procurement contracts awarded during the period and raised questions regarding certain tender conditions and concessions reportedly provided in some states.

However, the report stated that it did not find evidence of illegal conduct and noted that securing all eight tenders does not, by itself, establish wrongdoing.

Responding to the findings, the Adani Group rejected the allegations and maintained that all contracts were obtained through transparent and competitive bidding processes conducted in accordance with applicable regulations and approved by relevant authorities.

The report has sparked discussion among policy observers, industry experts and political commentators regarding transparency in power procurement, competition in the energy sector and the growing role of private companies in India's electricity generation landscape.

The developments have also renewed debate on how large-scale energy contracts are awarded and monitored, particularly as India continues to expand its power infrastructure to meet rising energy demand.

The claims and responses are likely to remain part of a broader public discussion on governance, regulation and competition within the country's power sector.

title: MP Bishnu Pada Ray Hands Over MPLADS Pick-Up Vans to Sabri and Shivapur Gram Panchayats
author: Dweep Tulika
description: MP Bishnu Pada Ray hands over two MPLADS-sanctioned pick-up vans to Sabri and Shivapur Gram Panchayats for garbage collection and sanitation.
html:
Mayabunder:

Hon’ble Member of Parliament for the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Shri Bishnu Pada Ray, handed over two pick-up vans sanctioned under the Members of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) to Gram Panchayats Sabri and Shivapur at the Deputy Commissioner's Office in Mayabunder.

The handover took place in the presence of the Deputy Commissioner, Zilla Parishad members and representatives of the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs).

The two vehicles will be utilised by the respective Gram Panchayats for garbage collection and sanitation-related activities, according to the information released regarding the handover.

The initiative is intended to strengthen local waste-management facilities and improve the ability of the two panchayats to carry out regular garbage collection.

The vehicles are also expected to support cleanliness and sanitation efforts in the respective panchayat areas and contribute towards maintaining a cleaner environment for local residents.

The provision of dedicated vehicles for waste collection is particularly relevant to rural local bodies, where the availability of appropriate transportation can support the regular collection and disposal of household and community waste.

The handover represents an intervention at the local-government level aimed at strengthening basic sanitation infrastructure in Sabri and Shivapur Gram Panchayats.

Editorial note

This report is based on the information provided regarding the handover. No additional claims about the cost of the vehicles, date of sanction, procurement agency, individual vehicle specifications or exact MPLADS project details should be added unless supported by official records.

title: TSG Aura Resort Hosts Special Lunch for Students of Government Middle School, Sitapur
author: Dweep Tulika
description: TSG Aura Resort hosted a special lunch for students of Government Middle School, Sitapur, Shaheed Dweep, as part of its CSR initiative.
html:
Shaheed Dweep | August 2026

As part of its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives, TSG Aura Resort hosted a special lunch for the students of Government Middle School, Sitapur, Shaheed Dweep.

The initiative was aimed at creating a warm and memorable experience for the young students while encouraging meaningful interaction between the resort team and the local school community.

During the occasion, the team spent time with the children, interacted with them and shared moments of joy.


Beyond providing a meal, the initiative offered an opportunity to engage with the students and make them feel valued, appreciated and cared for.

Through such community-focused CSR initiatives, TSG Hotels & Resorts continues to contribute towards the well-being of local communities and promote positive social impact in the Islands.

title: India Ranks 176th Out of 177 in 2026 Environmental Performance Index
author: Dweep Tulika
description: India ranks 176th of 177 countries in the 2026 EPI with a score of 22.46, while ranking 175th in air quality.
html:
New Delhi | 11 August 2026

India has been ranked 176th out of 177 countries in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index (EPI), recording an overall score of 22.46 out of 100, according to the latest assessment by the Yale Center for Environmental Law & Policy in collaboration with Columbia University.

The 2026 EPI assesses 177 countries using 47 indicators across 12 issue categories, grouped under three broad policy objectives: Environmental Health, Ecosystem Vitality and Climate Change.

India's performance was particularly weak in environmental health and air quality. The country ranked 174th in Environmental Health, with a score of 15.13, while its Air Quality ranking stood at 175th, with a score of 7.89.

Despite its low overall position, India's EPI score has increased by 7.47 points over the 10-year period covered by the index. The EPI's country data records India as having a 10-year change of +7.47.

Within the Southern Asia grouping, India ranked eighth among eight countries. Bhutan ranked first in the region, followed by Sri Lanka, Nepal, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Maldives and Bangladesh, with India at the bottom of the regional table.

The findings point to continuing challenges related to air quality and broader environmental health, while other components of environmental performance also contribute to India's overall score. For example, India ranked 174th in Biodiversity & Habitat, with a score of 9.09.

The EPI is a composite assessment rather than a single measurement of environmental conditions. Its results are intended to provide a comparative assessment of national environmental performance against established policy targets. The 2026 EPI also provides country-level data, trends and indicator scores for more detailed analysis.

India's 176th position therefore places the country near the bottom of the 2026 global ranking, while its positive 10-year score change indicates improvement on the index's measurement scale over the period.

Source: 2026 Environmental Performance Index, Yale Center for Environmental Law & Policy.

title: Mass Resignations Shake ABVP in Andaman; Student Leaders Cite Concerns Over Functioning
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Eight ABVP office-bearers in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands resign together, citing concerns over organisational functioning, autonomy and student repr
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair), Andaman & Nicobar Islands | 25 July 2026

In a significant development in the student politics of the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, eight office-bearers and members of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) have collectively resigned from their respective posts and primary membership of the organisation with immediate effect. The resignation letters were addressed to the President of the ABVP Nagar Unit, Sri Vijaya Puram, with copies forwarded to the State President, State Secretary, and Nagar Secretary.

The resigning members are Ayush Raj (Nagar Media Convener), Nikhil Parmar Singh (ALC Unit Secretary), Sneha Priya Das (ALC Unit President), Kushal Mondal (Executive Member), Ayushi Alok Reddy (Member, TGCE Unit Committee), Himanshu Kumar (Joint Secretary, ALC Unit), Afreen Kamil (Executive Member, ALC Unit), and Nitin Bepari (Joint Secretary).

According to the resignation letters, the members said the decision followed considerable reflection on their experiences within the organisation. They stated that they had joined ABVP with the intention of serving student welfare, strengthening student representation, and contributing to nation-building. However, they alleged that committed workers were not provided sufficient opportunities to participate meaningfully in organisational activities, leading to disappointment and frustration.

The former office-bearers also expressed concern over what they described as the increasing involvement of professors and other non-student individuals in organisational affairs. They claimed such involvement compromised the independence and autonomy expected of a student organisation and weakened democratic student representation.

The resignation letters further state that although ABVP presents itself as a non-political student organisation, the members had increasingly come to believe that its functioning reflected support for a particular political organisation. They said this perception conflicted with the principles on which they had chosen to associate themselves with the organisation.

The members also expressed dissatisfaction with what they described as the organisation's response during periods when students required collective leadership and decisive action. They stated that they did not witness the level of commitment and leadership they had expected from an organisation representing student interests, and that this experience played a significant role in their decision to resign.

Despite their criticisms, the former members thanked colleagues and office-bearers who had supported and guided them during their tenure. They acknowledged the experience gained through their association with ABVP and conveyed their best wishes for the organisation's future.

With the resignations taking immediate effect, all eight individuals have relinquished their organisational responsibilities and ceased to be primary members of ABVP. At the time of publication, there was no official response from ABVP regarding the resignations or the issues raised in the letters

title: TSG Bhasker Visits Flood-Hit Areas in North & Middle Andaman, Reviews Relief Measures
author: Dweep Tulika
description: TSG Bhasker visited flood-affected areas from Kadamtala to Mayabunder and reviewed relief and rehabilitation measures.
html:
Shri TSG Bhasker, Chairman of the Campaign Committee of the Andaman & Nicobar Territorial Congress Committee (ANTCC), undertook an extensive three-day visit to several flood-affected areas across North and Middle Andaman to assess the damage caused by recent heavy rains and flooding.

The visit covered multiple villages and settlements between Kadamtala and Mayabunder, where Shri Bhasker reviewed the ground situation and interacted with residents affected by the floods.

During the visit, he met affected families, visited inundated households and listened to firsthand accounts of the difficulties being faced by local residents. He assured the affected people that the Congress party stands with them during this challenging period and would raise their concerns before the appropriate authorities.

As part of the tour, Shri Bhasker also met the Assistant Commissioner of Rangat and held discussions regarding immediate relief measures, rehabilitation efforts and the need for timely assistance to families that have suffered losses due to the floods.

He emphasized the importance of ensuring that all affected households receive adequate support and compensation at the earliest.

Expressing concern over the recurring impact of heavy rainfall in the region, Shri Bhasker highlighted the need for a comprehensive long-term strategy to mitigate flood-related risks.

He urged the administration to focus on strengthening drainage systems, improving water flow channels and implementing sustainable infrastructure measures aimed at preventing similar situations in the future.

During the visit, Shri Bhasker also interacted with PRI members, community leaders and local residents to understand the challenges arising from the recent floods and to discuss measures for improving disaster preparedness and response mechanisms.

The visit formed part of ongoing efforts to assess the impact of the recent flooding and facilitate necessary support for affected communities across North and Middle Andaman.

title: Donald Trump Urges U.S. to “Move On” From Epstein Files Controversy
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Donald Trump said the United States should “move on” from the Epstein files controversy following recent document releases.
html:
Washington, D.C., March 2026:

Former U.S. President Donald Trump has stated that it is time for the United States to “move on” from issues related to the Jeffrey Epstein case.

The remarks came during an interaction with a CNN reporter following the latest release of documents by the U.S. Department of Justice connected to the Epstein case.

The comments come amid continuing scrutiny of the Epstein files, with survivors, advocacy groups, and sections of the media continuing to demand accountability and transparency regarding the case.

title: ANIIDCO and the Question of Government Revenue, Where Should Public Commercial Power Serve Islanders?
author: Dweep Tulika
description: ANIIDCO operates across milk, petroleum, liquor and tourism. The bigger question is how government commercial activity should serve Islanders.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | August 26, 2026

The Andaman & Nicobar Islands has a unique economic challenge. Its geography makes many essential services expensive to provide, while its small and scattered population can make several commercial activities difficult for private companies to operate profitably.

That is one reason government intervention remains necessary.

But there is another side to the question.

The Andaman & Nicobar Islands Integrated Development Corporation Limited (ANIIDCO) is a government-owned corporation that does not merely perform administrative functions. Its stated objective includes developing and commercially exploiting the natural resources of the territory for balanced and environmentally friendly development.

This raises an important public-policy question:

When a government corporation participates in commercial activities and generates revenue, where is that commercial role justified—and how should Islanders benefit from it?

ANIIDCO Was Created for Development, Not Simply Revenue Collection

ANIIDCO was incorporated in 1988, with a mandate covering infrastructure and development in sectors including tourism, fisheries and industries, as well as financial assistance to industrial and service units.

It would therefore be inaccurate to describe ANIIDCO simply as a mechanism created to collect money from Islanders.

Its stated purpose is broader.

A government corporation can intervene where private investment is inadequate, develop infrastructure, support local industries, serve remote communities and undertake projects that may have wider economic benefits.

The question is therefore not whether such a corporation should exist.

The question is how its commercial role should be measured and justified.

Milk: Revenue and Public Welfare Can Coexist

ANIIDCO's dairy operations provide one example.

The corporation collects raw milk from farmers in South Andaman, Shaheed Dweep and North & Middle Andaman and sells products including toned milk, paneer and curd in the local market.

The Administration has previously reported that when ANIIDCO increased the procurement price paid to farmers, milk procurement increased substantially and farmers' monthly income also rose.

This is the kind of government commercial intervention that can have a defensible public purpose.

The government is not merely selling milk.

It can potentially provide farmers with an assured market, strengthen local production and improve availability for consumers.

So the relevant question is not:

“Why is the government selling milk?”

It is:

“Is the government's involvement producing a measurable benefit for farmers and consumers, and is that benefit worth the public resources involved?”

Petroleum Shows Another Reason for Government Participation

ANIIDCO also operates petroleum retail outlets.

When the Administration established outlets at Baratang and Uttara, it stated that the objective was to ensure availability of an essential service to people in remote areas and reduce difficulties faced by residents and commuters.

The two outlets brought ANIIDCO's petroleum retail/depot network to 13 at the time.

This illustrates why government participation in a commercial market cannot automatically be labelled inappropriate.

If a private operator does not find a remote location commercially attractive, government intervention may be necessary.

The government can therefore have two different roles:

Commercial operator where the market fails.

Regulator where the market works.

The challenge is knowing which role is appropriate in each sector.

Liquor Raises a Different Question

Liquor provides a more direct example of government participation in a revenue-generating commercial market.

ANIIDCO operates IMFL outlets, and a 2026 government e-procurement listing confirms an ANIIDCO–IMFL organisational chain.

An RTI-based report published in 2024 stated that ANIIDCO's IMFL stores recorded combined gross sales of more than ₹181 crore during calendar year 2023.

That figure should not be confused with profit or net government revenue.

Sales turnover is not the same as profit.

Nevertheless, it demonstrates the scale at which a government corporation can participate in a commercial consumer market.

This leads to a legitimate accountability question:

If a government corporation has the organisational capacity to operate a large commercial distribution network, how should the returns from that activity be accounted for, and what public purpose should they ultimately serve?

That is a question of accountability—not an allegation of wrongdoing.

Tourism Is Another Major Area

ANIIDCO has historically been involved in tourism infrastructure and hospitality.

Government records describe its role in tourism development, including the operation and expansion of resorts.

ANIIDCO also appears as the tendering authority for major tourism projects. For example, a 2026 government tender for a five-star eco-tourism resort at Smith Island was issued through ANIIDCO on a PPP basis.

Government participation in tourism can have a legitimate development rationale.

Tourism infrastructure can create employment, attract investment and expand opportunities outside already-developed tourist centres.

But the same principle applies:

Public involvement should produce a demonstrable public benefit.

So Where Does the Revenue Go?

This is where the debate should become more serious.

When a government corporation generates commercial turnover, citizens deserve to understand the difference between:

  • Gross sales
  • Operating expenses
  • Taxes and duties
  • Subsidies
  • Capital expenditure
  • Borrowing
  • Depreciation
  • Operating profit or loss
  • The eventual financial return to the government

A ₹100-crore turnover does not mean the government earned ₹100 crore.

Likewise, a government corporation making a loss does not automatically mean an activity has failed if it is deliberately providing an essential service to remote communities.

The correct assessment requires looking at the complete financial and public-service picture.

ANIIDCO's annual accounts are subject to statutory reporting and have been laid before Parliament along with the Auditor's Report and CAG comments, providing an established mechanism for financial scrutiny.

That is precisely the mechanism through which citizens and legislators should examine whether commercial activities are delivering value.

Revenue Generation Should Not Become the Only Objective

There is nothing inherently wrong with a government corporation earning revenue.

If a public corporation can provide a useful service, support local producers and generate income without imposing an unnecessary burden on taxpayers, that can be a positive outcome.

But a government corporation is not a private company.

Its success should therefore not be judged solely by:

“How much money did it make?”

It should also be judged by:

“What public problem did it solve?”

Did it support local farmers?

Did it make essential commodities available in remote areas?

Did it attract investment?

Did it create employment?

Did it improve tourism infrastructure?

Did it serve communities where private operators would not?

And, most importantly:

Could the same public objective have been achieved more efficiently?

This Is Where Essential Services Enter the Debate

The Andaman & Nicobar Islands still requires substantial public investment in healthcare, drinking water, electricity, education, transport, telecommunications, roads, disaster preparedness and inter-island connectivity.

These are fundamentally different from ordinary commercial markets.

A resident can choose whether to buy a particular brand of milk.

A person cannot choose whether an emergency hospital exists when they need one.

A tourist can decide whether to stay at one resort or another.

A remote resident cannot simply choose an alternative electricity network if there is only one available.

A customer can decide whether to purchase a commercial product.

A child cannot postpone education indefinitely because providing a school in a remote settlement is expensive.

That is the fundamental difference between commercial choice and public necessity.

The question is therefore not:

“Why is ANIIDCO making money?”

The better question is:

“What is the government doing with its capacity to make money, and is that capacity being matched by its responsibility to provide essential public services?”

ANIIDCO's commercial activities can be justified when they address market failures, support local producers, provide essential supplies to remote areas or advance broader development objectives.

But those justifications should be transparent.

Every major commercial activity should have a clear public purpose, measurable outcomes and financial accountability.

And where an activity exists primarily for revenue generation, citizens have a legitimate right to ask why the government is the appropriate operator and what benefit Islanders receive from it.

The Standard Should Be Simple

The government does not need to withdraw from every commercial activity.

Nor does every government corporation have to operate at a profit.

But public money and public institutions should be directed according to public priorities.

If government intervention makes milk available while increasing farmers' income, that is a measurable public benefit.

If government-operated petroleum outlets ensure supplies in remote areas where private business may not serve, that is a measurable public benefit.

If tourism projects create sustainable employment and investment, that benefit should be measurable.

If a commercial activity generates substantial revenue, its financial performance should be transparent.

And if the government is spending or investing public resources, Islanders should be able to see the cost, return and public benefit.

That is not an attack on ANIIDCO.

It is the standard that any public institution should be willing to meet.

The Real Question for Andaman & Nicobar

The debate should move beyond the simplistic argument that “government should not do business.”

Government sometimes has to enter markets precisely because the market cannot adequately serve the Islands.

But neither should commercial revenue become an excuse to overlook the government's fundamental responsibilities.

The real question is one of priority and accountability:

Where government intervention is necessary, let it be strong. Where the private sector can deliver efficiently, let it participate. Where a government corporation earns revenue, let the accounts be transparent. And where essential public services remain inadequate, let those services receive the priority that only government can guarantee.

ANIIDCO can be an instrument of development.

But ultimately, the measure of a government corporation should not simply be how much money it generates.

It should be how effectively it converts public authority, public assets and public investment into public benefit.

Dweep Tulika | A Truthful & Unbiased Perspective

title: CBSE to Introduce Third Language from Class 6 Under NEP 2020
author: Dweep Tulika
description: CBSE will introduce a third language from Class 6 under NEP 2020 from the academic session 2026–27.
html:
New Delhi, 26 February 2026:

The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) will introduce a third language from Class 6 beginning with the academic session 2026–27, in accordance with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2023.

Under the proposed framework, students will study three languages, with at least two being Indian languages. According to official sources, English will be treated as a foreign language under the new structure.

Schools currently offering English in Class 6 may continue doing so, provided students also study two Indian languages. Similarly, foreign languages such as French or German may be offered only alongside two Indian languages.

The framework further recommends continuation of all three languages up to Classes 9 and 10. Reports suggest that from the 2031 Class 10 Board examinations onwards, students may also be required to appear for examinations in the third language.

CBSE is presently preparing learning materials in several Indian languages, including Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada, Gujarati, and Bangla. Detailed implementation guidelines are expected to be issued soon.

Additional instructional time has also reportedly been allocated during Classes 6 to 8 to support effective learning of the third language.

The initiative aims to promote multilingualism and strengthen students’ connection with India’s linguistic and cultural diversity.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume VIII, Issue No. 12, dated 20 March 2026.

title: TSG Bhasker Urges Centre to Regulate Sky-High Airfares for Andaman & Nicobar Islands
author: Dweep Tulika
description: TSG Bhasker urges the Civil Aviation Ministry to cap airfares, increase flights and protect islanders from exorbitant ticket prices.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram, July 11:

Shri TSG Bhasker, Chairman of the Campaign Committee of the Andaman & Nicobar Territorial Congress Committee (ANTCC), has written to the Union Minister for Civil Aviation, urging immediate intervention to regulate the high airfares charged by airlines operating between the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and major mainland cities.

In his representation, Shri Bhasker stated that airfare on routes connecting Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair) with Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata, Visakhapatnam and other mainland destinations has become unaffordable for ordinary citizens. Referring to his own recent travel experience, he said a one-way journey from Delhi to Port Blair for two passengers cost ₹73,662, highlighting what he described as the alarming escalation in ticket prices.

He argued that it is unreasonable for Indian citizens to pay more for domestic travel to the Andaman & Nicobar Islands than for international flights to several foreign destinations. According to him, such pricing places an excessive financial burden on island residents while also discouraging tourism and affecting visitor arrivals.

Shri Bhasker emphasized that the people of the islands rely almost entirely on air transport for higher education, specialized medical treatment, employment, business and family emergencies. Students studying on the mainland and patients requiring advanced medical care in cities such as Chennai, Kolkata and Delhi are among those most affected by the rising airfare.

He further pointed out that many families are forced to spend enormous amounts to transport critically ill patients by air, including stretcher cases, with some reportedly selling their properties to meet travel expenses. He described the situation as financially devastating for residents of a Union Territory where air connectivity serves as the primary lifeline.

Questioning the absence of airfare regulation, Shri Bhasker observed that while the government fixes Maximum Retail Prices (MRP) for essential commodities such as packaged drinking water, there is no ceiling on airline fares despite air travel being an essential service for island residents. He also expressed concern that airlines often reduce flight frequencies during the off-season, limiting seat availability and contributing to higher ticket prices.

In his letter, Shri Bhasker requested the Ministry of Civil Aviation to:

  • Direct airlines to maintain affordable fares throughout the year.
  • Fix a maximum ceiling on airfares for routes connecting the islands with mainland cities.
  • Increase flight frequencies and encourage greater competition among airlines.
  • Introduce concessional fares for patients travelling for medical treatment.
  • Operate additional chartered flights during peak travel seasons to meet passenger demand.

He stated that air travel for the people of the Andaman & Nicobar Islands is not a luxury but an essential public service, expressing hope that the Ministry would take prompt action to protect the interests of lakhs of island residents and tourists from excessive airfare burdens.

title: Trump Warns Iran to Honour Deal, Says U.S. Will Act if Commitments Are Violated
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Trump warned that the U.S. will act if Iran fails to honour the interim agreement reached during recent peace negotiations.
html:
U.S. President Donald Trump has warned that Washington will take necessary action if Iran fails to comply with the terms of the recently agreed interim deal aimed at reducing tensions in the Middle East.

Washington, June 23:

U.S. President Donald Trump has warned that the United States will take necessary action if Iran fails to honour the commitments made under a recently negotiated interim agreement aimed at easing tensions and paving the way for a broader peace settlement in the Middle East.

Speaking to reporters, Trump said Iran must strictly comply with the terms of the agreement, adding that Washington would closely monitor its implementation.

"If they don't stick to the deal, we'll do what we have to do," Trump said, reaffirming that while diplomacy remains the preferred path, the United States is prepared to respond if the agreement is violated.

The remarks come shortly after Washington announced limited sanctions relief as part of ongoing diplomatic efforts to encourage further negotiations with Tehran.

The interim agreement follows recent talks in Switzerland between senior U.S. and Iranian officials. U.S. Vice President JD Vance earlier described those discussions as having laid a "good foundation" for a comprehensive peace agreement.

According to officials, both sides have agreed to continue technical-level negotiations in the coming weeks, focusing on issues such as regional security, maritime stability, nuclear oversight and sanctions.

Despite signs of diplomatic progress, significant differences remain over key issues, including the scope of sanctions relief, Iran's nuclear programme and broader regional security arrangements.

Analysts believe the success of the peace process will ultimately depend on whether both countries honour their commitments and maintain constructive dialogue.

Trump's latest remarks underscore Washington's intention to balance diplomatic engagement with a firm stance on compliance as negotiations continue.

title: Student’s Speech on Equality and Justice Draws Attention at Andhra Pradesh School Event
author: Dweep Tulika
description: A student’s speech on equality, justice, and civic responsibility at an Andhra Pradesh school event gained widespread attention.
html:
Palnadu, Andhra Pradesh, 26 January 2026:

A student of ABC CBSE School in Andhra Pradesh delivered a powerful speech on equality, justice, and civic responsibility during a school event, earning widespread appreciation from the audience.

The institution, established in 1982, is regarded as the first English-medium school in the Palnadu region.

Opening with the line, “I do not stand here to comfort you, I stand here to disturb you,” the student emphasized that republics weaken not because of external threats, but when citizens stop questioning injustice.

Referring to the ideals of the Constitution of India, the speech questioned whether equality before law is genuinely practiced in society. The student highlighted issues such as gender bias, caste discrimination, and prejudice based on appearance, pointing towards the gap between constitutional values and everyday social realities.

The speech also addressed societal hypocrisy, stating that while equality is taught in classrooms, discrimination often continues in daily life.

“We celebrate equality on paper, but practice discrimination in reality,” the student remarked.

Calling for greater civic awareness and moral courage, the speaker argued that justice and equality cannot survive through institutions alone and require active participation from citizens.

The speech concluded with a message urging introspection and responsibility among individuals: “Stop asking what the Republic can do for you, start asking what you are doing for the Republic.”

The address was widely appreciated for its clarity, conviction, and relevance, with many describing it as a strong reflection on democracy, citizenship, and social responsibility.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume VIII, Issue No. 12, dated 20 March 2026.

title: NEET UG 2026 Re-Test Conducted at Three UAE Centres for Eligible Candidates
author: Dweep Tulika
description: NTA conducted the NEET UG 2026 re-test at three centres in the UAE under enhanced security and examination protocols.
html:
The National Testing Agency conducted the NEET UG 2026 re-test at three designated centres in the United Arab Emirates under enhanced security arrangements.

New Delhi, June 21:

The National Testing Agency (NTA) conducted the NEET UG 2026 re-test on Sunday, June 21, at three designated examination centres in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

The re-examination was conducted as part of the NEET UG 2026 re-test process announced by the NTA. The examination was held in pen-and-paper mode under enhanced security and monitoring arrangements.

The three designated centres in the UAE were:

• The Indian High School, Dubai
• Sharjah Indian School, Sharjah
• Abu Dhabi Indian School, Abu Dhabi

Candidates appearing for the examination were required to carry their admit cards, valid identification documents and comply with all examination-day guidelines issued by the NTA.

According to official advisories, special arrangements were made to ensure a smooth, fair and secure conduct of the examination. Strict entry procedures, verification protocols and examination guidelines were implemented across centres.

The re-test forms part of the agency's efforts to maintain transparency, fairness and equal opportunity in one of India's largest medical entrance examinations.

NEET UG serves as the gateway for admission to undergraduate medical, dental and AYUSH courses across the country and is among the largest entrance examinations conducted by the National Testing Agency.

Following the completion of the examination, the NTA is expected to proceed with evaluation, answer-key publication and result preparation according to its official schedule.

The agency has reiterated its commitment to conducting examinations in a secure and transparent manner while ensuring that eligible candidates receive a fair opportunity to compete.

title: ‘Colours of India 2026’ to Showcase Renowned Classical Artists in Sri Vijaya Puram
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Colours of India 2026 will bring renowned Indian classical music and dance artists to Sri Vijaya Puram on August 13.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram, 12 APRIL 2026:

A grand cultural evening celebrating Indian classical music and dance titled “Colours of India 2026” is scheduled to be held in Sri Vijaya Puram on August 13, bringing together several nationally acclaimed artists and performers under one stage.

The programme will commence from 5 PM onwards at the Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Auditorium in Sri Vijaya Puram, Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

The event is being organised by Swaranjali Delhi in association with NrityaMalancha, while Mukta Dhara Society is serving as the local coordinator. Organisers described the initiative as one of the largest independently coordinated classical cultural programmes hosted in the islands in recent years.

Several eminent artists from across the country are expected to perform during the evening, including noted sitar exponent Pt. Subrata De, tabla artist Pt. Susamoy Mishra, vocalist Shri Bhutnath De from Jharkhand, vocalist Shri Partha Sarathi Lenka from Odisha, and Shri Mridul Nath along with Smt. Sikha Mahanta Nath from Assam.

The programme will also feature performances by Guru Vidushi Sangita Chaki ji, Bharatnatyam exponent Smt. Sobha Devi R.V. and disciples of Daksh Dance Akademi, along with a group Bharatnatyam presentation by Vikash Akademi. Pune-based Bharatnatyam performer Ms. Rajasi Wagh is also scheduled to perform.

In addition to visiting artists, several local performers and cultural groups including Daksh Dance Akademi and NrityaMalancha Group will participate in the programme, creating a cultural confluence representing diverse Indian classical traditions.

According to organisers, the initiative aims to preserve and promote India’s rich cultural heritage while encouraging local students, performers, and art enthusiasts through direct exposure to nationally respected artists.

Dweep Tulika News has been named as the media partner for the event, while Shreyas WebMedia Solutions will serve as the online media partner.

The programme will remain open to the public without entry fees, and organisers have invited residents and media representatives to attend the event.
