title: Australia Sues Amazon Over Prime Video Advertising Changes
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Australia's consumer watchdog has sued Amazon, alleging Prime Video advertising changes breached consumer protection laws.
html:
Canberra, June 30:

Australia's competition regulator has initiated legal proceedings against Amazon's Australian subsidiary, alleging that the company breached consumer protection laws by introducing advertisements on its Prime Video streaming service after customers had already paid for annual Prime memberships.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) claims that more than one million Australian consumers who subscribed to Amazon Prime for A$79 per year were affected when advertisements were introduced on Prime Video. According to the regulator, customers were later required to pay an additional A$2.99 per month to continue watching content without advertisements.

The ACCC argues that Amazon altered a key feature of the subscription after consumers had already entered into annual contracts. It has also questioned whether contractual terms allowing such changes may be unfair under Australian consumer law.

The regulator is seeking financial penalties, declarations from the Federal Court, compensation or other remedies for affected consumers, and court orders preventing similar practices in the future.

Amazon Australia has acknowledged the legal proceedings and stated that it is reviewing the case. The company said it had cooperated with the ACCC during the investigation and will present its response through the court process.

Amazon Prime is a bundled subscription service offering Prime Video, faster delivery on eligible purchases, Prime Gaming and other digital services. In recent years, several streaming platforms worldwide have introduced advertising-supported subscription models while offering ad-free viewing at an additional cost.

Consumer rights groups have argued that companies should not substantially alter services already purchased under long-term subscriptions without providing adequate notice or obtaining meaningful consumer consent.

Legal experts believe the case could become an important test of how far digital platforms can modify subscription benefits after customers have signed annual contracts. A ruling in favour of the ACCC could strengthen consumer protections, encourage greater transparency and influence regulation of digital subscription services in other countries.

The Federal Court's decision is expected to be closely watched by consumer advocates, technology companies and streaming platforms worldwide, as it may establish an important precedent for digital subscription contracts.

title: ABVP Seeks Central University for Andaman & Nicobar, Calls for Review of Higher-Education Restructuring
author: Dweep Tulika
description: ABVP has sought a Central University for Andaman & Nicobar and called for review of NSCBIHL restructuring and higher-education policies.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | 11 August 2026

The Andaman & Nicobar Islands unit of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) has submitted a six-page memorandum to Vice-President of India and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha C. P. Radhakrishnan, seeking intervention on higher education, youth opportunities and long-term development in the Islands.

The memorandum, dated 8 August 2026, places the establishment of a full-fledged Central University in the Union Territory among its principal demands.

According to ABVP, geographical isolation limits access for students to specialised higher education, advanced research facilities, professional courses and employment opportunities. The organisation has proposed an island-specific higher-education model connecting education and research with employment, healthcare, tourism, the blue economy, environmental studies and strategic development.

Central University remains principal demand

ABVP states in its memorandum that it has been pursuing the demand for a Central University since 2006. It cites limited availability of undergraduate, postgraduate and doctoral programmes, specialised faculty and research infrastructure, as well as the financial and logistical burden of mainland travel, among the reasons for its demand.

The organisation has called for a publicly funded Central University specifically designed around the requirements of the Islands.

The proposed institution, according to the memorandum, should offer affordable higher education, modern academic programmes, scholarships, hostels, digital and library infrastructure, research facilities, industry linkages and entrepreneurship opportunities.

The demand comes as the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Institute of Higher Learning (NSCBIHL) has begun admissions for the 2026–27 academic session, indicating that its deemed-university framework is now being operationalised.

Review sought over NSCBIHL restructuring

ABVP has also raised concerns over the restructuring of higher education under NSCBIHL.

The organisation has referred to the proposed merger of seven government higher-education institutions and called for a transparent, evidence-based and time-bound review and consultation process before major structural decisions are taken.

It has sought participation from students, teachers, parents, academic experts, elected representatives, Panchayati Raj institutions, civil society and tribal representatives.

ABVP argues that the long-term institutional structure should be evaluated on the basis of accessibility, affordability, research capacity and the geographical and socio-economic conditions of the Islands.

Reservations over private university proposal

The memorandum also expresses reservations regarding the proposed Andaman & Nicobar Islands Private University Regulation, 2026.

ABVP has argued that private or self-financing institutions should not become a substitute for a publicly funded Central University.

The issue has also featured in the wider political debate. MP Bishnu Pada Ray had previously urged the Lieutenant Governor to keep the proposed Private University Regulation in abeyance and reiterated the demand for a Central University.

ABVP's memorandum similarly calls for a strong public higher-education system, with a Central University serving as its academic nucleus.

Youth employment, skills and healthcare

Beyond the university demand, ABVP has sought expansion of professional and vocational courses, skill-development programmes, entrepreneurship and start-up support, incubation centres, apprenticeships, career counselling, competitive-examination preparation, digital learning centres and research fellowships.

It has also sought greater employment opportunities for qualified local residents in higher-education institutions and development projects.

On healthcare, the organisation has called for expansion of tertiary healthcare, modern diagnostic infrastructure, specialist services, telemedicine, emergency and trauma care, improved access in remote islands and stronger nursing, paramedical and allied-health education.

Tribal studies and strategic research

The memorandum proposes dedicated academic programmes covering tribal studies, anthropology, indigenous knowledge systems, cultural documentation, biodiversity-linked traditional knowledge and sustainable development, while emphasising constitutional safeguards and tribal rights.

ABVP has also highlighted the strategic location of the Islands and proposed academic expertise in areas including maritime security, ocean governance, strategic and defence studies, disaster management, maritime logistics, coastal security, the blue economy and Indo-Pacific studies.

Proposed Island Knowledge and Development Ecosystem

ABVP has proposed an integrated model combining:

Education + Research + Connectivity + Employment + Healthcare + Tourism + Blue Economy + Environment + Strategic Development.

The organisation describes this as an "Island Knowledge and Development Ecosystem", under which students could pursue education, research, skills and entrepreneurship within the Islands rather than being compelled to leave for mainland institutions.

The memorandum concludes with eight principal requests, including establishment of a Central University, adequate Central funding and academic autonomy, review of the existing NSCBIHL restructuring, wider stakeholder consultation, strengthening of government colleges, improved youth employment and entrepreneurship opportunities, stronger tertiary healthcare and research addressing the Islands' ecological, geographical, strategic and socio-economic challenges.

The latest memorandum adds ABVP's voice to an ongoing debate over the future structure of higher education in the Union Territory.

The central question now concerns which model should form the long-term foundation of higher education in the Islands — the existing deemed-university framework, private-university possibilities, or a publicly funded Central University designed specifically for Andaman & Nicobar.

The implications extend beyond institutional status to access to higher education, research opportunities, employment and the broader developmental trajectory of the Union Territory.

Source: Memorandum submitted by Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, dated 8 August 2026.

title: AAP Rebuilds in Andaman & Nicobar: Dr. Arun Malik Unveils Local Governance, Jobs and Public-Issue Agenda Ahead of 2027 Elections
author: Dweep Tulika
html:
29 Aug 2026, Sri Vijayapuram:

The Aam Aadmi Party has announced a fresh organisational push in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, with newly appointed State President Dr. Arun Kumar Mallik outlining a broad political and governance agenda at a public meeting held at Tiranga Park.

The meeting marked what party leaders described as a renewed beginning for the AAP's organisation in the islands, which, according to the speakers, had remained largely inactive for several years.

Dr. Mallik was introduced as the party's newly appointed State President for Andaman and Nicobar, with the appointment dated August 10, 2026. In his address, he said the immediate objective was not merely to expand the party politically but to build an organisation capable of identifying and taking up everyday problems faced by residents with the local administration.

The meeting therefore went beyond an organisational announcement. Dr. Mallik used the platform to lay out a wide-ranging list of issues that he said would form the party's priorities in the islands from healthcare and education to employment reservation, roads, transport, water, tourism, land conversion, street vendors, drug abuse, environmental concerns and alleged corruption.

From a dormant organisation to a grassroots campaign

Dr. Mallik said the AAP's presence in the islands had become largely dormant over the previous five to six years and that his immediate task was to rebuild it at the grassroots.

He said the party intended to establish an organisational structure extending from the district level down to tehsil, panchayat and village levels. Coordinators would be identified at each level, with particular emphasis on bringing young and educated people into politics.

He described the party's stated organisational principles as patriotism, honesty and humanity, while presenting what he called "alternative politics" as a model in which elected representatives remain focused on resolving people's problems rather than merely raising them.

According to Dr. Mallik, an elected representative whether a panchayat member, councillor or MP should function as a problem-solver for citizens.

He cited a recent complaint from Diglipur concerning STS bus online ticketing as an example. According to his account, residents contacted him after the online ticketing system had reportedly stopped functioning for about two weeks, after which the matter was taken up with the local administration. He presented this as an example of how the party intended to work on day-to-day public grievances.

95% local employment reservation emerges as a major demand

One of the strongest policy positions articulated during the meeting was the demand for 95% reservation for local people in employment.

Dr. Mallik argued against what he described as an impractical demand for 100% reservation, while advocating a 95% model. He referred to Ladakh as an example and said the party would pursue a similar framework for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

He also raised questions concerning the distinction between Islanders' status, residence certificates and other categories of local documentation. The speech referred to different groups of settlers and residents and argued that employment benefits should be structured in a manner that protects the interests of local people.

The issue, he said, would be taken up with the administration and the Lieutenant Governor and, where necessary, pursued at the Union Government and parliamentary level.

Healthcare: focus on specialists, rural facilities and management

Healthcare was another major component of the speech.

Dr. Mallik argued that the island's healthcare system should not be portrayed as uniformly poor, saying that several government services were functioning and that recent improvements had taken place. At the same time, he pointed to shortages of specialist doctors, GDMOs, nurses, laboratory personnel and other staff as areas requiring attention.

He called for additional Urban Health Centres and said the expansion of urban areas had not been matched by a corresponding expansion of primary healthcare facilities.

He also identified Diglipur and Ferrargunj as areas where additional PHCs were needed and raised the requirement for strengthening healthcare infrastructure in remote locations including Campbell Bay, Katchal and Billiground.

The availability of doctors in remote and tribal areas was another concern. Drawing on his own professional experience, Dr. Mallik argued that some locations which previously had full-time medical officers were now increasingly dependent on periodic field visits.

He also spoke about specialist shortages in hospitals in Mayabunder, Rangat and Diglipur and said that he had raised the matter with the administration.

GB Pant Hospital and ANIIMS

A substantial portion of his healthcare discussion concerned GB Pant Hospital and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands Institute of Medical Sciences (ANIIMS).

Dr. Mallik explained that the administrative structures governing GB Pant and the other district and community health facilities were different, and argued that residents needed to know which authority was responsible when they faced problems.

He described the separation of responsibilities between the health services administration and ANIIMS as an important management development and credited former Chief Secretary Keshav Chandra with understanding the issue and supporting changes in the management structure.

He also acknowledged recent specialist appointments and said that the administration had taken steps to strengthen healthcare delivery.

Roads and NH-4: questions over delays and accountability

Road infrastructure featured prominently in the meeting.

Dr. Mallik questioned the prolonged construction of National Highway-4 and argued that despite years of work, sections remained incomplete. He also raised allegations of irregularities in road construction and called for greater scrutiny of the agencies and contractors involved.

He criticised the condition of municipal roads in Port Blair and alleged that repeated road works raised questions regarding accountability among municipal engineers, contractors and other agencies. These were presented as political allegations at the meeting and were not independently established in the speech.

The party's position, according to Dr. Mallik, is that infrastructure projects should be monitored more closely and that public representatives should actively question delays and implementation problems.

Weigh bridges, overloading and road safety

The issue of vehicle overloading was also discussed.

Dr. Mallik said the operation of weigh bridges was important both for road safety and for protecting roads from damage. He referred to concerns raised by transport operators and drivers and said that after the issue was brought before the administration, action was taken.

He argued that weigh bridges should function effectively and that additional facilities may be required in different parts of the islands.

The speech also referred to maritime transport and the need to ensure that vessels comply with safety and carrying-capacity requirements before passengers or cargo are permitted to board.

Inter-island connectivity remains a concern

For an archipelago dependent heavily on sea and air connectivity, transport between islands was presented as a major public-service issue.

Dr. Mallik said the existing inter-island helicopter service was not sufficient to meet the needs of the population. He acknowledged the role played by emergency services, including the Navy and Coast Guard, in medical emergencies but argued that regular civilian connectivity required greater attention.

The broader argument was that residents outside Port Blair should not be disadvantaged simply because of their geographical location.

Water supply and infrastructure gaps

Water supply was also discussed as part of the broader infrastructure agenda.

Dr. Mallik linked water-related problems to the wider question of how infrastructure projects are implemented and monitored, arguing that projects should not merely be shown as completed on paper while residents continue to face shortages or service gaps.

The criticism was directed at what he described as a gap between administrative records and conditions experienced on the ground.

Education: deemed university controversy and student concerns

Higher education occupied a significant section of the meeting.

Dr. Mallik recalled the student movement against the proposed transition of the institution into a deemed university. According to his account, students began protesting in February, following which he wrote to the then Chief Secretary seeking continuation of the students who had joined in 2025 under Pondicherry University rather than being shifted into the new arrangement.

He said the administration subsequently took up the issue and that permission was obtained from the Government of India for the students' continuation.

At the same time, he criticised what he described as misinformation and political appropriation of the student movement, arguing that the original student concerns should have remained the central focus.

He also raised the shortage of hostel accommodation for students coming from North and Middle Andaman and other areas outside Port Blair, saying that students without hostel facilities are forced to spend more on private accommodation.

Private universities: regulation before expansion

On the recently proposed framework for private universities, Dr. Mallik took a position that was more supportive of regulation than outright opposition.

He said the administration's proposed regulation should first be studied before political parties reject it. According to him, a private university could potentially create employment and educational opportunities, but a regulatory framework should be in place before any institution is established.

He said he had studied the proposed regulation in detail and submitted comments to the administration. Among the recommendations he mentioned were requirements concerning faculty strength, including assistant professors, associate professors and professors, as well as greater representation of non-official members on expert committees.

He further recommended that a large share of non-teaching employment generated by a future private university should go to local residents.

He also welcomed provisions concerning reservation for Scheduled Tribes and OBCs and suggested greater involvement of independent experts and civil-society representatives in regulatory committees.

Vocational education and ITIs

Dr. Mallik argued that the debate around education should not stop at universities and colleges.

He referred to the islands' vocational and industrial training institutions and alleged shortages of qualified directors, lecturers and other technical personnel.

According to him, strengthening ITIs and vocational training centres, including hostel facilities, should be part of the party's education agenda. He also linked vocational institutions to the wider need for drug-free campuses.

Drug abuse: concern over school-level availability

Drug abuse was described as another serious issue facing the islands.

Dr. Mallik said he had heard reports of drugs being supplied to school students, while acknowledging that he did not possess documentary evidence for some of the claims he mentioned.

He said the administration and law-enforcement agencies were already pursuing a "zero tolerance" approach and referred to the Drug-Free Andaman and Nicobar initiative. However, he argued that enforcement and awareness efforts needed to go further, particularly where drugs may be reaching school students.

He also said that awareness programmes alone would not be sufficient and called for members of the public to report suspected drug distribution through appropriate channels.

Street vendors: rights along with compliance

Street vending was presented as another important livelihood issue.

Dr. Mallik referred to registered street vendors in the Port Blair Municipal Council area and said vendors had rights that needed to be protected.

At the same time, he urged vendors to operate only in designated areas and not occupy non-vending zones. He said a survey had recently been conducted and that those eligible under the rules could receive licences, including people who had not been able to participate in the earlier survey.

He emphasised that the issue should not be framed as a conflict between islanders and non-islanders, arguing that people come to the islands from different parts of the country in search of livelihoods.

Allegations concerning illegal migration and certificates

One of the more politically sensitive sections of the speech concerned what Dr. Mallik described as illegal migration.

He alleged that foreign nationals entering the islands illegally were, in some cases, being provided documents including residence certificates or Islanders-related documentation through corrupt practices.

He specifically referred to alleged involvement of some panchayat representatives and municipal councillors and said that cases had been registered against some individuals in the past. He claimed to possess documentary evidence concerning several cases.

These statements were made by Dr. Mallik during the meeting and constitute allegations; the transcript itself does not independently establish the claims or identify official findings in each case.

He also distinguished between foreign nationals and internal migrants from mainland India, arguing that the two categories should not be treated in the same manner.

Land conversion: criticism over policy uncertainty

Land conversion was another issue raised from the perspective of residents and landholders.

Dr. Mallik said conversion of agricultural land to other uses had been restricted since 2019 and welcomed what he described as the administration's recent move to restart the process.

However, he criticised what he portrayed as uncertainty in the policy, saying that residents had at different times been told that conversion was closed and later that it had reopened, without clear communication of the relevant orders.

He cited his own experience of applying for conversion as an example of the difficulties faced by applicants.

His broader demand was for a clear, transparent and officially documented conversion process.

Voter-list revision becomes an electoral concern

The Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls was also discussed.

Dr. Mallik raised concerns over the number of names removed from the electoral rolls in the islands and said residents had contacted him after discovering that their names were no longer present.

Importantly, he also acknowledged the work of Booth Level Officers and said he believed the administration had undertaken the exercise carefully. His concern, he said, was specifically about residents whose names may have been deleted unintentionally.

He urged affected residents to approach the party so that their cases could be pursued through the prescribed process before the deadline he cited, in preparation for the expected local-body elections.

He further claimed that a large proportion of the deletions were concentrated in the Port Blair area and linked the issue to questions surrounding residence certificates, electoral registration and local political representation. Those wider allegations remain claims made during the meeting and would require independent documentary verification.

Environment and indigenous rights

Environmental protection and indigenous rights were another important element of the address.

Dr. Mallik referred to the scale of environmental damage that could result from large infrastructure projects and spoke about the need to protect indigenous communities and their rights.

He referred to environmental-impact assessment procedures and alleged that certain reports or processes had not been carried out correctly, including claims of pressure and inaccurate reporting. He also welcomed what he described as international attention to indigenous rights and environmental concerns.

His position was not presented as opposition to all infrastructure development. Rather, he argued that major projects should avoid entering areas inhabited or used by indigenous communities and suggested that infrastructure such as airports and ports should be located in appropriate areas.

Death cases and demand for investigation

Dr. Mallik also referred to two murder cases, including the death of Anish Toppo and the killing of a media professional identified in the transcript as "Shahdev".

On the Anish Toppo case, he clarified that, at the time of the meeting, a CID investigation by the Andaman and Nicobar Police was underway and that he was awaiting its report. He said he hoped the investigation would provide satisfactory answers.

He also questioned the status of the other murder investigation and called for greater public accountability in such cases.

A different approach to political opposition

A notable feature of Dr. Mallik's address was his argument that the AAP would not automatically oppose every initiative of the administration.

Using the proposed private-university regulations as an example, he said political parties should read and understand government proposals before opposing them. If a policy was beneficial, he said, it should be supported; where it was flawed, the party would raise objections.

This approach, he said, was part of the party's "alternative politics" model.

Port Blair and airport naming proposals

The meeting also included a cultural and political identity component.

Dr. Mallik said that if the AAP eventually came to power in the islands, it would seek to restore the name "Port Blair" and also proposed renaming Veer Savarkar International Airport after John Richardson, whom he described as an early Nicobari MP.

These were presented as future political commitments rather than immediate administrative decisions.

The six-month electoral push

The speech ultimately returned to organisation and elections.

Dr. Mallik described the coming six months as crucial for the party because of the expected local-body elections. He said the AAP intended to campaign at the district, tehsil, panchayat and village levels.

He said the party already had four people willing to contest municipal elections and that it intended to identify young and energetic candidates.

The party also plans, according to the speech, to undertake visits across North and Middle Andaman, Nicobar and South Andaman as part of its grassroots campaign.

The stated political proposition is therefore broader than simply contesting elections: the party wants to establish itself as an organisation that handles day-to-day public grievances while simultaneously building a candidate base for the 2027 local elections.

AAP's message: administration should be engaged, not simply opposed

One of the more significant themes running through the entire meeting was the relationship the party says it wants with the administration.

Dr. Mallik repeatedly said that many public problems could only be solved by working with the local administrative system. He spoke positively about several officials and acknowledged initiatives undertaken by the administration, even while criticising other decisions and demanding greater accountability.

That position represents a somewhat different political pitch from conventional opposition politics: support measures considered beneficial, question decisions considered inadequate, and attempt to resolve individual grievances through administrative engagement.

From public meeting to political test

The Tiranga Park meeting was therefore less a single-issue political gathering and more an attempt by the revived AAP leadership to establish a broad political narrative for the islands.

Dr. Mallik's speech combined immediate public grievances healthcare shortages, transport difficulties, roads, education and water with longer-term political questions involving employment reservation, land policy, environmental protection, indigenous rights, electoral rolls and local governance.

At the organisational level, the party has set itself an ambitious target: rebuilding its presence from the district to the village level and identifying candidates ahead of the 2027 local-body elections.

At the policy level, it has placed employment reservation, public healthcare, education, infrastructure and accountability at the centre of its message.

And at the political level, it is presenting itself as an alternative that, in its own words, intends to put the "common man" at the centre of governance.

Whether that message translates into a sustained grassroots organisation and ultimately into electoral support will become clearer as the party moves from public meetings and issue-based interventions to its proposed village-level campaign and candidate selection ahead of the local-body elections.

Editorial Note: This report is based on Dr. Arun Kumar Mallik's address at the AAP public meeting at Tiranga Park and the corresponding YouTube Live/transcription studied by Dweep Tulika. Political positions, allegations and claims made during the meeting have been attributed to the speaker. Where independent documentary verification was not available from the material reviewed, such claims have not been presented as established facts.

title: Tiruvallur Ammonia Leak Tragedy: Death Toll Rises, Probe Ordered as PM Modi Expresses Grief
author: Dweep Tulika
description: An ammonia gas leak at a seafood processing unit in Tamil Nadu's Tiruvallur district has claimed multiple lives and injured dozens.
html:
Several workers were killed and dozens hospitalised after an ammonia gas leak at a seafood processing facility in Tamil Nadu's Tiruvallur district.

Tiruvallur/New Delhi, June 21:

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has expressed deep grief over the loss of lives following a tragic ammonia gas leak at a seafood processing facility in Tamil Nadu's Tiruvallur district.

The incident occurred at a seafood export unit near Periyapalayam in Tiruvallur district, where ammonia gas reportedly leaked from an industrial refrigeration system used for seafood preservation.

According to reports, the leak affected a large number of workers present at the facility. Initial reports indicated two deaths, but later updates suggested that the death toll had risen to seven. More than 60 workers were reportedly hospitalised after suffering breathing difficulties and other symptoms associated with ammonia exposure.

Many of the affected workers were migrant labourers employed at the processing unit. Emergency response teams, ambulances and police personnel rushed to the site and shifted victims to nearby hospitals for treatment.

Ammonia is widely used in industrial refrigeration systems but can be highly dangerous when released in large quantities. Exposure may cause severe respiratory distress, eye irritation, lung damage and, in extreme cases, death.

Expressing condolences, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he was deeply pained by the loss of lives and prayed for the speedy recovery of those injured.

Following the incident, Tamil Nadu authorities ordered an inquiry into the circumstances that led to the leak. A committee has reportedly been constituted to investigate the cause of the accident and examine whether safety protocols were followed.

The tragedy has once again drawn attention to industrial safety standards and emergency preparedness at facilities handling hazardous substances.

Authorities are continuing their investigation, and casualty figures may be updated as official verification progresses.

title: Maharashtra Tightens Marathi Language Checks for Auto, Taxi and App-Based Cab Drivers
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Maharashtra intensifies Marathi language checks for auto, taxi and app-cab drivers, with oral tests, notices and possible badge suspension.
html:
Mumbai | August 23, 2026

The Maharashtra government has intensified enforcement of its Marathi language requirement for autorickshaw, taxi and app-based cab drivers, with Regional Transport Office (RTO) teams conducting checks across the state.

Under the latest enforcement drive, drivers are being assessed on their basic working knowledge of Marathi through a 16-question oral test based on situations they commonly encounter while working.

Drivers who fail to demonstrate adequate proficiency are being issued notices and given one month to improve their language skills. Continued non-compliance could result in suspension of their driver badges.

The enforcement follows a 105-day training and assessment programme. As of August 16, around 7,750 drivers had failed the proficiency test, while another 17,427 had not completed the required training.

On the first day of the statewide checking drive, more than 8,200 drivers were assessed, with 1,268 issued notices for failing to meet the language requirement. However, in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, approximately 85% of drivers tested on the first day passed.

The government has said the requirement is intended to ensure smoother communication between drivers and passengers.

The enforcement has nevertheless sparked debate, particularly because a similar Marathi-language requirement linked to autorickshaw permits was struck down by the Bombay High Court in 2017.

Meanwhile, commuters in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region are also set to face higher fares from September 1, with autorickshaw fares increasing by ₹1 and taxi fares by ₹2.

The latest enforcement drive places language proficiency, transport regulation and commuter costs at the centre of renewed debate over public transport in Maharashtra.

title: Peak-Hour Road Repair Raises Safety Concerns at Chandni Chowk–Andaman Castle Road
author: Dweep Tulika
description: A Dweep Tulika ground report examines road repair work at Chandni Chowk–Andaman Castle Road, where peak-hour construction has raised commuter safety
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair), Andaman & Nicobar Islands | 30 July 2026

Road repair work on the Chandni Chowk–Andaman Castle Road has raised concerns among commuters after the final seal coat was laid during peak morning traffic on Wednesday.

According to observations made by the Dweep Tulika team, repair work on the damaged stretch began in early July with road levelling and other preparatory works. However, the final seal coat was not laid at that time, leaving the road unfinished for nearly 15 days.

When the work resumed on 30 July, the seal coat was laid during the busiest hours of the morning, when students, office-goers and daily commuters were using the road. Intermittent rainfall combined with loose dust on the unfinished surface created slippery conditions. During the course of the work, the Dweep Tulika team observed multiple two-wheelers skid and fall while negotiating the stretch.

The team also observed that potholes had already developed on portions of the road before the final seal coat was applied, prompting commuters to question the quality and sequencing of the repair work.

While residents welcomed the ongoing maintenance, several questioned whether such operations could instead be scheduled during late-night or other low-traffic hours. They said this would reduce inconvenience, improve commuter safety and allow roadwork to be carried out more efficiently.

The incident highlights the importance of not only repairing roads but also ensuring that public works are executed with proper planning, traffic management and quality control to minimise risks to road users.

title: Mangoes, Markets and Mixed Signals: What Happened After PM Modi's Mann Ki Baat?
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Days before Japan suspended Indian mango imports and Nepal tightened checks, PM Modi praised India's mango growers in Mann Ki Baat.
html:
New Delhi, 01 June 2026:

In the 134th episode of Mann Ki Baat on 31 May 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised India's mango growers and highlighted the global recognition enjoyed by Indian mangoes.

Calling mangoes an important part of India's culture and agricultural identity, the Prime Minister credited farmers for helping Indian varieties gain popularity both within the country and abroad.

However, even as the praise was being delivered, the 2026 mango season was facing significant challenges.

Japan Suspends Indian Mango Imports

Earlier in March 2026, a Japanese quarantine inspection team visited Indian Vapour Heat Treatment (VHT) facilities and reportedly identified deficiencies in pest-control and disinfection procedures.

Japanese authorities later announced that mango consignments certified on or after 25 March 2026 would not be accepted until corrective measures were implemented.

On 29 May 2026, Japan suspended imports of fresh Indian mangoes for the remainder of the 2026 season.

The affected varieties included:

  1. Alphonso
  2. Kesar
  3. Banganapalli
  4. Langra
  5. Chausa
  6. Malika

Japanese authorities stated that the issue was related to quarantine and phytosanitary compliance rather than pesticide contamination.

Nepal Tightens Import Requirements:

During April and May 2026, concerns were raised in Nepal regarding pesticide residues in imported mango consignments.

Reports on 9 and 10 June suggested that Nepal had banned Indian mangoes. Nepal later clarified that imports had not been completely stopped but would be subject to stricter quality-control and phytosanitary requirements.

Weather Adds To Farmers' Problems:

The 2026 season also brought weather-related difficulties for growers.

Several mango-producing regions reported lower yields due to adverse climatic conditions. In parts of Maharashtra's Alphonso-producing belt, some local assessments reported severe crop losses in affected areas.

The combination of reduced production and export restrictions has increased pressure on farmers, traders and exporters during the peak season.

India's Major Commercial Players:

India remains the world's largest mango producer.

Some of the country's prominent commercial players in the mango sector include:

  1. Reliance Industries (Dhirubhai Ambani Lakhibag Amrayee, Jamnagar)
  2. IG International
  3. Kay Bee Exports
  4. KK Star Exports
  5. Shreevali Agro

The Bigger Picture:

The developments of 2026 highlight both the strengths and vulnerabilities of India's mango industry.

While Indian mangoes continue to enjoy global recognition and strong domestic demand, growers and exporters remain exposed to weather disruptions, international quality standards and changing trade regulations.

As India seeks to expand agricultural exports, maintaining compliance with international quarantine requirements may become as important as increasing production itself.

Source: Publicly available government statements, quarantine notifications, trade reports and media coverage.

title: Pondicherry University Students’ Council Opposes Transfer of Andaman Colleges
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Students’ Council of Pondicherry University opposes transfer of Andaman colleges, citing concerns over higher education access.
html:
Pondicherry, 25 February 2026:

The Students’ Council of Pondicherry University (2025–26) has strongly opposed the Union Government’s reported decision to transfer the affiliation of seven colleges in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands from Pondicherry University.

Comrade Syed Inayat Hussain, General Secretary of the Students’ Council and member of the Students Federation of India (SFI), stated in a video message that the move could isolate students of the islands and weaken their access to quality public higher education under a Central University system.

He further pointed out that the islands already lack premier national institutions such as IITs and IIMs, and argued that the proposed decision may further marginalize students instead of improving educational opportunities.

“The elected Students’ Council of Pondicherry University strongly condemns this decision and stands in solidarity with the students and people of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands,” Hussain stated while demanding immediate withdrawal of the move.

The statement adds to the growing opposition from student bodies and stakeholders regarding the proposed restructuring of higher education institutions in the islands.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume VIII, Issue No. 12, dated 20 March 2026.

title: SFI AMU Opposes Transfer of Andaman Colleges from Pondicherry University
author: Dweep Tulika
description: SFI AMU has opposed the transfer of Andaman colleges from Pondicherry University, extending solidarity with island students.
html:
Uttar Pradesh, 07 March 2026:

The Students Federation of India unit of Aligarh Muslim University (SFI AMU) has strongly condemned the Central Government’s decision to transfer the affiliation of seven government colleges in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands from Pondicherry University.

In a statement, Mehrin Rehman, President of SFI AMU, said that students of the islands are already geographically isolated and rely on affiliation with a Central University for access to quality higher education.

She stated that the proposed decision could weaken students’ academic opportunities and further isolate learners from remote island regions.

“SFI AMU strongly condemns this move and stands in complete solidarity with the students of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. We demand an immediate rollback of the decision,” she said.

Rehman further emphasized that education is a right and urged authorities to reconsider the decision in the interest of students from remote regions.

The statement adds to the growing opposition from student organizations across the country regarding the proposed change in affiliation of colleges in the islands.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika print edition dated 20 March 2026.

title: DAE Inaugurates Deuterated Compounds Plant, Commissions Prototype Sodium Cell in Vadodara
author: Dweep Tulika
description: DAE inaugurated a deuterated compounds plant and commissioned a prototype sodium cell to boost India's nuclear programme.
html:
The Department of Atomic Energy has inaugurated a new deuterated compounds production facility and commissioned a prototype sodium cell to strengthen India's nuclear and scientific capabilities.

Vadodara, June 21:

In a major boost to India's scientific and strategic capabilities, the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) inaugurated the Versatile Deuterated Compounds Production Plant (VDPP) and commissioned a 24 kA Prototype Sodium Cell at the Heavy Water Board Facilities (HWBF) in Vadodara, Gujarat.

The facilities were inaugurated by Dr. Ajit Kumar Mohanty, Secretary, Department of Atomic Energy and Chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission.

The newly established VDPP is designed to strengthen India's indigenous production of specialised deuterated compounds, which are widely used in advanced scientific research, strategic applications and emerging technologies. The facility will help meet national demand for high-purity deuterated solvents through domestic production.

A key highlight of the event was the commissioning of the 24 kA Prototype Sodium Cell, a major technological milestone towards indigenous industrial-scale production of nuclear-grade sodium. The material plays a crucial role in India's Fast Breeder Reactor Programme, which forms the second stage of the country's three-stage nuclear power strategy.

Speaking on the occasion, Dr. Mohanty said the two facilities reflect India's growing capability to develop critical technologies through indigenous research, engineering and innovation. He noted that the projects will contribute to strategic self-reliance, advanced scientific research and the long-term objectives of India's nuclear energy programme.

The event was attended by senior officials of the Department of Atomic Energy, Heavy Water Board scientists, engineers and technical personnel.

Officials stated that the developments reinforce the vision of AtmaNirbhar Bharat and support India's journey towards becoming a technologically advanced and self-reliant nation.

The inauguration marks another important step in strengthening India's strategic materials programme and enhancing domestic capabilities in critical scientific and nuclear technologies.

title: MP Bishnu Pada Ray Lays Foundation Stones for Road Development Projects in Sri Vijaya Puram
author: Dweep Tulika
description: MP Bishnu Pada Ray laid foundation stones for road renovation and resurfacing works across nine locations in Sri Vijaya Puram.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram, 14 March 2026:

Bishnu Pada Ray laid the foundation stones for renovation and resurfacing works of link roads at nine locations across the municipal area of Sri Vijaya Puram, South Andaman, under the Central Road Fund (CRF) Phase-I project.

The locations covered under the development initiative include School Line (Ward 15), Dairyfarm (Ward 15), School Line (Ward 16), Dollygunj (Ward 17), Brookshabad (Ward 22), Carbyn’s Cove (Ward 21), Austinabad (Ward 20), Garacharma (Ward 19), and Birdline (Ward 23).

According to official information, an amount of ₹1 crore has been sanctioned for each municipal ward to undertake road renovation and infrastructure improvement works.

The MP expressed gratitude towards the Government of India and the Union Territory Administration for supporting the initiative and facilitating the allocation of funds under the Central Road Fund scheme.

He stated that the projects are expected to improve road conditions, strengthen connectivity, and ensure safer travel for residents across several parts of South Andaman.

The initiative is also expected to contribute towards better local infrastructure and smoother transportation within the municipal region.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume VIII, Issue No. 12, dated 20 March 2026.

title: Sonam Wangchuk's Hunger Strike Enters 18th Day as Health Concerns Mount
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Sonam Wangchuk's hunger strike entered Day 18 at Jantar Mantar as health concerns grew and the Delhi High Court examined a PIL.
html:
NEW DELHI, July 16: 

Social reformer and education activist Sonam Wangchuk's indefinite hunger strike at Jantar Mantar entered its 18th day on Thursday, with concerns over his health increasing and renewed calls for dialogue between the protesters and the Central Government.

Wangchuk joined an ongoing student-led protest on June 28. According to protest organisers, the movement seeks greater transparency and accountability in India's recruitment and entrance examination system following allegations of examination irregularities. Protesters have also demanded comprehensive examination reforms and the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The protest has drawn participation from students, youth organisations, civil society groups and several public figures. Opposition leaders and various organisations have expressed support for the agitation, while others have appealed to Wangchuk to end his fast because of his deteriorating health.

According to updates shared by those associated with the protest, Wangchuk has experienced significant weight loss and increasing physical weakness during the prolonged fast. Medical professionals have continued to monitor his condition. Wangchuk has maintained that the protest will remain peaceful and has said meaningful dialogue is necessary to address the demonstrators' concerns.

The matter has also reached the judiciary. The Delhi High Court has sought responses from the Central Government and the Delhi Government after a Public Interest Litigation requested urgent medical intervention in view of Wangchuk's health condition.

No formal resolution had been announced at the time of publication. The Central Government had not issued any fresh public response to the latest demands of the protesters that could be independently verified. As the hunger strike continues, developments at Jantar Mantar are expected to remain under close public and judicial scrutiny.

title: The Great Nicobar Debate
author: Dweep Tulika
description: The Great Nicobar Project continues to spark debate over development, ecology, tribal concerns and India’s strategic future.
html:
Development, Strategy and Ecological Concerns

Sri Vijaya Puram | May 30, 2026 
A remote island. A mega infrastructure project worth over ₹70,000 crore. A location close to one of the world’s busiest maritime trade routes. And a debate that continues to intensify across strategic, environmental and public circles.

Great Nicobar, once known primarily for its dense rainforests, biodiversity and indigenous communities, is now emerging at the centre of one of India’s most ambitious development visions.

The proposed Great Nicobar Project includes a transshipment port, international airport, power infrastructure, township development and connectivity expansion aimed at transforming the island into a major maritime and logistics hub in the Indian Ocean region.

Supporters of the project describe it as a strategic opportunity for India.

They argue that the project could strengthen India’s maritime presence near the Malacca Strait, reduce dependence on foreign transshipment hubs such as Singapore and Colombo, improve regional connectivity, generate employment and accelerate economic activity in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

Strategic experts have also highlighted the increasing importance of the Indian Ocean region amid evolving geopolitical dynamics and growing maritime competition across Asia.

However, the project has also generated serious environmental and social concerns.

Great Nicobar is home to ecologically sensitive rainforests and several protected species, including the endangered Leatherback Sea Turtle and the Dugong, the State Animal of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Environmental groups and researchers have raised concerns regarding large-scale construction activity, deforestation, coastal impact and long-term ecological sustainability.

Questions have also been raised regarding the Shompen tribe, one of India’s Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs), whose traditional habitat exists within parts of the island.

The memory of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami has further intensified public discussion surrounding the scale and long-term implications of large infrastructure expansion in the region.

The Government has maintained that environmental safeguards, rehabilitation measures and tribal protections are part of the proposed framework and that development and conservation can progress together through regulated planning and monitoring.

As discussions continue, the Great Nicobar Project is increasingly becoming more than just an infrastructure proposal. It represents a larger national conversation about development, environmental responsibility, strategic security and the future direction of island regions.

The Great Nicobar Project continues to generate discussion across environmental, strategic and developmental circles, reflecting the broader challenge of balancing national growth with ecological responsibility.

This article is part of Dweep Tulika’s ongoing special coverage series on the Great Nicobar Project and its implications for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

title: Pentagon Releases Hundreds of UFO Files, Renews Debate Over Unexplained Aerial Sightings
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Pentagon releases declassified UAP files, reigniting debate over unexplained aerial sightings and military observations.
html:
Washington, May 10, 2026:

The United States Department of Defense has released more than 170 declassified files related to unidentified flying objects (UFOs), now officially referred to as unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAPs), renewing global discussion surrounding decades of unexplained aerial sightings.

The document release follows ongoing transparency initiatives by US authorities regarding unexplained aerial incidents observed over several decades.

According to reports, the released files include accounts dating back to the 1940s involving civilians, commercial pilots, police officers, military personnel and astronauts. The documents reportedly contain observations of unusual aerial objects and unexplained flight behaviour, though no official confirmation regarding extraterrestrial origins has been provided.

Among the earlier accounts referenced in the files is a 1947 report from California in which a farmer allegedly witnessed a hovering object emitting sparks and flames before rapidly disappearing from sight. Other documents reportedly describe sightings involving glowing objects, flying discs and unexplained aerial movements across different parts of the United States.

One report from 1950 described an alleged incident involving police officers in Philadelphia who claimed to have observed a glowing object descending into a field. According to the document, the object reportedly appeared to disintegrate shortly after the officers approached the site.

The files also contain accounts involving aviation personnel. A 1947 report filed by pilots aboard a Pan American aircraft described cylindrical flying objects allegedly travelling at high speed near their flight path. Additional records reference observations reported by US Navy pilots and astronauts during various missions.

One notable entry relates to the 1965 Gemini 7 mission, during which astronauts Frank Borman and Jim Lovell reportedly observed unidentified objects and particles while in orbit. Internal notes attached to the files described the incident as a possible “UFO sighting.”

More recent documents reportedly include infrared footage and military pilot observations recorded during training exercises and aerial patrol operations. Several reports describe objects moving at unusual speeds or appearing stationary despite strong winds, behaviour that pilots considered inconsistent with known aircraft systems.

Despite the release of the files, US authorities have not confirmed the extraterrestrial origin of any reported phenomenon. Officials stated that the records are being made public as part of a broader transparency initiative, with additional files expected to be released gradually.

The publication of the documents has once again intensified global public interest in UFOs and unexplained aerial activity, subjects that continue to attract attention from defence agencies, researchers and governments worldwide.

title: India Targets 100 GW Pumped Storage Capacity as Hydropower Emerges as ‘Water Battery’: IHA Report
author: Dweep Tulika
description: India plans to build 100 GW of pumped storage hydropower by 2035-36 to strengthen renewable energy and grid stability.
html:
India plans to develop 100 GW of pumped storage hydropower by 2035-36 as global focus shifts towards energy storage solutions supporting renewable power.

Guwahati, June 24:

India is aiming to develop 100 gigawatts (GW) of pumped storage hydropower capacity by 2035-36, according to the 2026 Global Hydropower Outlook released by the International Hydropower Association (IHA).

The report describes pumped storage hydropower as a "water battery", highlighting its growing importance in storing surplus electricity generated from renewable sources such as solar and wind and supplying power when demand increases.

Unlike conventional batteries, pumped storage plants store energy by pumping water to an elevated reservoir during periods of excess electricity generation. When electricity demand rises, the stored water is released through turbines to generate power, helping stabilise the electricity grid.

According to the report, India's proposed expansion is expected to play a crucial role in supporting the country's renewable energy ambitions, improving grid reliability and reducing dependence on fossil fuels.

The outlook also noted that China continues to lead global hydropower development, with more than 300 GW of hydropower capacity currently under construction, including around 218 GW of pumped storage projects.

While India's planned expansion represents one of the world's largest future pumped storage programmes, experts say faster project execution, investment and supportive policies will be essential to achieve the target.

The report further highlighted that East Asia remains the global leader in hydropower development, driven primarily by large-scale investments in China.

As India moves towards higher renewable energy adoption, pumped storage hydropower is expected to become a key component of the country's long-term energy security and clean energy transition.

title: Old Video of BJP MLA Yogesh Verma Assault Resurfaces Online, Misrepresented as Recent
author: Dweep Tulika
description: A viral video showing BJP MLA Yogesh Verma being assaulted is from October 2024, not a recent incident. Here's the verified context.
html:
Lakhimpur Kheri, Uttar Pradesh | 8 August 2026

A video showing BJP MLA Yogesh Verma being slapped and manhandled during a public altercation has once again gone viral on social media, with many users sharing it as a recent incident. However, available evidence indicates that the footage actually dates back to October 2024 and relates to a dispute during the Lakhimpur Urban Cooperative Bank election process in Uttar Pradesh.

The confrontation occurred during the nomination process for the cooperative bank elections in Lakhimpur Kheri, where tensions had reportedly escalated between rival groups supporting different candidates for the bank's governing body.
Videos from the incident show Yogesh Verma involved in a heated argument before he was allegedly slapped and physically manhandled in the presence of police personnel. Officers intervened and attempted to separate those involved before bringing the situation under control.

According to multiple media reports, the individual accused of assaulting the MLA was Advocate Awadhesh Singh, who was then serving as President of the Lakhimpur Bar Association. Reports stated that Singh was supporting the candidature of his wife, Pushpa Singh, while Yogesh Verma was backing a rival panel in the cooperative bank election.

Following the incident, Yogesh Verma alleged that BJP-supported candidates were prevented from filing nomination papers and claimed that nomination documents were torn before he was assaulted. He also denied allegations circulated by some individuals that he had arrived under the influence of alcohol.
Awadhesh Singh rejected the MLA's allegations and claimed that Yogesh Verma and his supporters had disrupted the nomination process. He alleged that the MLA repeatedly misbehaved with officials and others present. These competing accounts remain the respective versions of the parties involved.

The incident drew political attention at the time, with opposition parties criticising the law-and-order situation and BJP leaders condemning the assault on the sitting MLA. Reports subsequently indicated that the Urban Cooperative Bank election process was postponed.

Although the incident itself is genuine, there is no credible evidence that it occurred recently. The video circulating on social media is an old recording from October 2024, which has resurfaced without its original context.

title: Waybridge, Flights, Elections & Tourism: Dr Arun Mallik Answers Andaman’s Biggest Questions
author: Dweep Tulika
description: AAP Andaman President Dr Arun Mallik discusses weighbridges, airfares, tourism, healthcare, elections, NH-4 and other island issues.
labels: AAP Andaman President Dr Arun Mallik discusses weighbridges
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | August 12, 2026

By Dweep Tulika

AAP Andaman & Nicobar Islands State President Dr Arun K. Mallik addressed a wide range of issues concerning the islands in an interview with Dweep Tulika, including the operation and mandatory use of weighbridges, transportation challenges in North and Middle Andaman, electoral practices, healthcare, tourism development, airfares and higher education.

The interview covered several concerns raised by residents and transport operators, with questions focusing particularly on the difficulties faced by people living in geographically isolated areas of the islands.

Weighbridge operation and mandatory inspections

Dr Mallik said the issue of the weighbridge was brought to his attention by members of the truck and drivers' associations, who approached him regarding vehicles continuing to operate without consistently using the facility.

According to him, the weighbridge had remained unused for a considerable period before becoming operational. He said he subsequently visited the facility with his team and wrote to the administration seeking action.

Dr Mallik argued that regular use of the weighbridge could improve road safety, ensure vehicles carry permitted loads and make driving safer for drivers.

He further said that after the weighbridge became operational, some vehicle operators complained about fines and alleged inconsistencies in checking. He said some drivers were nevertheless supportive of the weighbridge because carrying excessive loads puts additional pressure on vehicles and drivers.

Dr Mallik said he had therefore requested that weighbridge inspection be made mandatory for all applicable vehicles, rather than relying only on periodic enforcement.

He also raised concerns over the practice of declaring one load quantity on documentation while allegedly carrying a higher quantity. He said mandatory weighing could help reduce such discrepancies and make enforcement more systematic.

More weighbridges along NH-4

Dr Mallik also called for additional weighbridges along NH-4, arguing that a single facility would not be sufficient for the entire North and Middle Andaman region.

He specifically mentioned the need for facilities around Diglipur, Mayabunder and Rangat, while suggesting that the precise locations should be determined on technical and administrative considerations.

He said additional weighbridges would make compliance more practical for vehicles operating across the region.

When asked whether additional weighing requirements and transportation-related costs could indirectly increase the cost of living for people in North and Middle Andaman, Dr Mallik acknowledged that costs could rise indirectly. However, he argued that this should not become a reason to disregard transportation and safety regulations.

Electoral awareness and alleged malpractices

The interview then turned towards elections and allegations of malpractice.

Dr Mallik said his experience of contesting an election gave him an understanding of the challenges involved in the electoral process. He said greater public awareness was necessary, particularly in villages and areas where voters may have less access to information.

He announced plans for an awareness campaign in which he and his team would visit villages over the coming months to discuss what is permitted and what is not permitted during elections.

According to Dr Mallik, the objective would be to help voters make informed decisions rather than dictate whom they should support.

When asked specifically about the message he would give to people in Diglipur and other isolated areas regarding alleged electoral malpractices, Dr Mallik urged voters not to exchange their vote for money or other inducements.

He said voters should make their choice based on the candidate they believe will work for them. He also made political comments about candidates of established parties and his own party's prospective candidates.

During the discussion, Vineeth challenged Dr Mallik on his statement regarding election-time monetary inducements. Dr Mallik responded that voters should make their own decision regardless of what they may be offered, stressing that accepting money or other items should not determine their vote.

Call for more impartial local media

Dr Mallik also spoke about the role of local media in creating public awareness.

He criticised what he described as partisan tendencies among sections of the media and argued that the islands need more independent and impartial reporting.

He said local media could play an important role in informing residents about issues in their villages, including problems with public services and healthcare.

As an example, he referred to a visit to Ramnagar where residents allegedly told him that a doctor was not regularly available at a local health sub-centre. He said he subsequently raised the matter with the health administration and claimed that an order had been issued concerning the issue.

Healthcare concerns in remote areas

Healthcare access emerged as another major issue during the discussion.

Dr Mallik referred to conversations with residents in rural areas who, according to him, face difficulties accessing doctors and healthcare services.

He argued that many of these problems are relatively small administrative issues that can nevertheless have a significant impact on residents when they are not addressed.

The discussion highlighted the importance of functioning health centres and regular availability of medical personnel, particularly for communities located away from the main urban centre.

Tourism beyond Swaraj Dweep and Shaheed Dweep

Vineeth questioned why tourism development remains heavily concentrated around Swaraj Dweep and Shaheed Dweep, despite the natural attractions of North and Middle Andaman.

He asked why improved connectivity and transportation could not be used to bring tourists to destinations such as Diglipur and other parts of the islands, thereby creating economic opportunities for local communities.

Dr Mallik agreed that tourism should be developed beyond the currently established destinations. He said North, Middle and Little Andaman should receive greater attention in tourism planning.

He also pointed to the importance of connectivity, noting that the proximity of Swaraj Dweep and Shaheed Dweep to the main tourism circuit makes them easier for visitors to access.

He argued that better connectivity could allow tourism benefits to reach communities farther from the capital and existing tourism centres.

Connectivity and dependence on sea routes

The interview also highlighted the broader transportation dependence of island communities.

Vineeth pointed out that many parts of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands remain dependent on transportation networks for essential supplies, healthcare and everyday necessities.

The discussion emphasised that transportation problems in remote areas can affect not only tourism but also the movement of food, medical needs and other essential goods.

The question of fixed airfares for islanders

Another major issue raised by Vineeth was the cost of air travel.

He questioned why islanders could not have a fixed or specially regulated airfare for travel between the islands and the mainland, particularly because air travel can become essential during medical emergencies and other urgent situations.

The discussion highlighted the unique geographical circumstances of the islands, where residents do not have a conventional road or rail alternative to reach the mainland.

Vineeth pointed to the financial burden faced by islanders who need to travel outside the islands for treatment or other urgent purposes. Dr Mallik agreed that tourism and connectivity policies need to account for the specific circumstances of island residents.

Can the Ladakh model offer lessons?

The conversation also touched upon the Ladakh model, particularly in relation to local employment and the ability of a Union Territory to seek arrangements that protect opportunities for its residents.

Dr Mallik referred to an example of job reservation in Ladakh and argued that the Andaman and Nicobar Islands' political representatives should pursue measures that could similarly benefit local residents.

He said the islands' status as a Union Territory gives its political representatives an important role in raising issues affecting the local population before the Centre.

Deemed university issue and protest

The interview also discussed the controversy surrounding higher education and the deemed university issue.

Dr Mallik criticised what he described as the failure of the earlier protest to continue with sufficient intensity. He said students had raised legitimate concerns but that the protest was subsequently diluted and withdrawn.

He said he had supported the students' demand and intended to take up the matter with the administration in his capacity as AAP state president.

Dr Mallik also questioned the process through which documents and reports relating to the university proposal were prepared and submitted, alleging that certain requirements had not been fulfilled. These allegations were presented as his claims during the interview and were not independently verified in the discussion.

Call for replacement of the Lieutenant Governor

Towards the end of the interview, Dr Mallik called for the replacement of the Lieutenant Governor of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, referring to the length of the incumbent's tenure.

He criticised aspects of the administration's planning priorities and argued that greater attention should be given to the needs of ordinary residents and communities outside the capital.

He also questioned proposals and development priorities in and around the urban area, arguing that some projects could instead be considered in North or Middle Andaman.

A broader discussion on the islands' future

The interview brought together a range of issues that directly affect everyday life in the islands—from transportation and road safety to healthcare, tourism, air connectivity, elections and higher education.

While Dr Mallik presented his political views and proposals as the newly appointed AAP state president, the discussion also reflected wider questions about how development can be distributed more evenly across the geographically dispersed islands.

For residents of North and Middle Andaman in particular, the questions of transportation, connectivity, healthcare access and tourism opportunities remain closely connected. Better infrastructure, reliable transportation and greater public awareness could influence both the economic opportunities available to remote communities and their access to essential services.

The complete interview is available on Dweep Tulika's YouTube channel, featuring Dr Arun K. Mallik responding to questions from Vineeth on the issues discussed above.

title: Supreme Court Clarifies Rules for Reserved Category Candidates in General Jobs.
author: Dweep Tulika
description: The Supreme Court has clarified that reserved category candidates can compete for general posts if selected purely on merit.
html:
New Delhi, 20 April 2026:

The Supreme Court of India has clarified a key aspect of recruitment policy, stating that candidates belonging to Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), and Other Backward Classes (OBC) are eligible to compete for general (unreserved) category government jobs, provided their selection is based purely on merit.

In its clarification, the court emphasized that if a candidate from a reserved category secures marks equal to or higher than the cut-off prescribed for the general category without availing any relaxation—such as age limits, application fee concessions, or qualification criteria—they must be treated as a general category candidate. The ruling reinforces the principle that merit-based selection should remain independent of social category when no reservation benefits are utilized.

However, the court also drew a clear distinction regarding the use of reservation benefits. It stated that if a candidate avails any form of relaxation or concession provided under reservation policies, they would not be eligible to claim a position in the general category. In such cases, their selection would remain confined to the reserved category under which they applied.

The clarification is expected to have significant implications for recruitment processes across government sectors, where confusion has often arisen regarding the classification of candidates who qualify on merit despite belonging to reserved categories. By reinforcing merit as the determining factor in such cases, the judgment aims to ensure both fairness and clarity in public employment systems.

Legal experts note that the decision strengthens the balance between reservation policies and merit-based competition, while also providing clearer guidelines to recruiting agencies. The ruling is likely to influence future recruitment notifications and selection procedures across various government departments.
