title: CISF Plans Integrated Facial Recognition Network for Airports and Strategic Installations
author: Dweep Tulika
description: CISF plans to link airport facial recognition cameras and 1.5 lakh surveillance cameras to a central data fusion centre.
html:
CISF plans to integrate facial recognition cameras at airports and nearly 1.5 lakh surveillance cameras at strategic locations into a central data fusion centre in Delhi.

New Delhi, June 23:

Facial recognition cameras installed at major airports across India and surveillance systems at key strategic installations are set to be integrated into a proposed central data fusion centre in Delhi, according to CISF Director General Praveer Ranjan.

The initiative aims to strengthen real-time surveillance, improve threat detection and enhance coordination among security agencies by linking facial recognition technology with the National Intelligence Grid (NATGRID).

Speaking during the foundation-laying ceremony of the new CISF headquarters at the CGO Complex in New Delhi, the CISF chief said that the proposed system will enable security agencies to identify suspects more efficiently and respond quickly to potential threats.

In addition to airport surveillance systems, video feeds from nearly 1.5 lakh CCTV cameras installed at vital installations protected by the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) across the country will also be connected to the data fusion centre.

Officials believe the integrated platform will provide a unified security network capable of analysing large volumes of surveillance data in real time, thereby strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure and other sensitive locations.

The project forms part of the government's broader efforts to modernise India's internal security architecture by leveraging advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, facial recognition and data analytics.

Once operational, the integrated surveillance network is expected to improve situational awareness, facilitate faster information sharing between agencies and reinforce security at airports and other strategic assets nationwide.

title: Heavy Rain Exposes Drainage Problems Across Sri Vijaya Puram
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Dweep Tulika's ground report highlights widespread waterlogging across Sri Vijaya Puram following heavy rain, raising fresh concerns over the city's d
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair), Andaman & Nicobar Islands | 3 August 2026

A spell of heavy rainfall on Monday led to widespread waterlogging across several parts of Sri Vijaya Puram, disrupting normal life and once again drawing attention to concerns over the city's drainage infrastructure. Although the rainfall was not considered exceptional by Andaman standards, several roads and public spaces were submerged due to poor drainage.

The Dweep Tulika team visited multiple affected locations, including the area in front of Hindi Sahitya Kala Parishad in Aberdeen Bazar, the premises of Jawaharlal Nehru Rajkeeya Mahavidyalaya (JNRM) and the Government Girls' Senior Secondary School campus. At all three locations, stagnant rainwater covered roads, footpaths and public areas, making movement difficult for pedestrians and motorists alike.

The waterlogging resulted in traffic congestion across several stretches of the city. Students, office-goers, shopkeepers and daily commuters faced considerable inconvenience, with many pedestrians forced to walk through knee-deep water to reach their destinations.

During the visit, several residents expressed concern over the recurring problem of waterlogging after rainfall. While many acknowledged the inconvenience caused by inadequate drainage, most preferred not to speak on record or have their views published.

Residents pointed out that the Andaman & Nicobar Islands have historically experienced much heavier rainfall than that witnessed on Monday. They questioned whether the existing drainage network is being adequately maintained and whether it remains capable of handling even moderate rainfall.

The incident has once again highlighted the importance of regular desilting, maintenance and timely improvement of urban drainage systems. Residents said that strengthening drainage infrastructure would not only reduce waterlogging but also minimise traffic disruption and improve public safety during the monsoon season.

title: When a Camera Becomes Evidence: Protecting Patient Privacy Without Silencing Public Accountability
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Dweep Tulika examines the debate over hospital videography, patient privacy, citizen evidence and public accountability after a request to restrict un
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | Public Interest Analysis

A request submitted by Dr Arun Kumar Mallik, Team Leader of the Aam Aadmi Party, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, to the Health Secretary has called for measures against what it describes as "unauthorized photography and videography" inside healthcare facilities of the Andaman & Nicobar Administration, including inpatient departments. The request refers to YouTubers, social-media influencers, journalists, patient attendants and politicians.

The request follows a video circulating on social media concerning the Sub-District Hospital, Diglipur. Dr Mallik alleges that the recording involved unauthorised videography, obstruction of a duty medical officer, an impact on patient privacy and dissemination of false information concerning the recently upgraded hospital. He has also sought appropriate action from the police and administration.

These are serious allegations and should be investigated rather than assumed to be established facts.

But the controversy raises another public-interest question: when does a camera become an intrusion, and when can it become evidence?

Patient privacy must remain protected

Hospitals are fundamentally different from ordinary public spaces. Patients may be undergoing treatment in vulnerable circumstances, medical records may be visible, and confidential conversations and procedures may take place.

Recording identifiable patients without consent, interfering with emergency treatment or obstructing medical personnel cannot be justified merely by invoking journalism or public interest.

Clear safeguards for patient privacy, medical confidentiality, dignity and uninterrupted healthcare are therefore necessary. Dweep Tulika supports such protections.

However, protecting privacy does not necessarily require treating every camera as a threat.

A mobile phone can be an individual's only record

For an ordinary citizen, a mobile phone camera can be more than a tool for social-media content. It can become the only contemporaneous record of an incident.

Consider a patient attendant who claims that a public official refused to provide a service, that a confrontation occurred, that inappropriate conduct took place, or that a public facility was functioning in a manner that raised serious concerns.

The subsequent dispute may become one version against another:

Citizen's account versus institution's account.

The individual may have no access to official CCTV footage, no independent witness may be willing to come forward, and official records may not capture everything that occurred.

In such circumstances, an original contemporaneous recording may become an important piece of documentation—and, in some cases, the person's last available record of what happened.

Any proposed restriction should therefore distinguish between intrusive recording of patients and documentation of an interaction or event involving the person making the recording.

Recording is not the same as publication

Another distinction is equally important.

Recording, preserving an original recording as evidence, and publishing that recording publicly are three different acts.

A citizen may record an interaction solely to preserve evidence and never publish it.

A journalist may record material for verification and subsequently decide that it should not be published.

A newsroom may receive a recording and withhold it after determining that publication could expose a patient's identity or confidential medical information.

Treating all three activities as one category of "videography" risks eliminating an important distinction.

Indian evidence law also recognises the legal significance of electronic and digital records. Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 provides that an electronic or digital record cannot be denied admissibility merely because it is electronic or digital, subject to Section 63. Section 63 provides statutory requirements concerning admissibility.

This does not mean every mobile-phone recording is automatically admissible evidence, nor does it establish an unrestricted right to record in every location.

It does, however, underline a basic reality:

Digital records can have evidentiary value.

The constitutional question is one of balance

Freedom of speech and expression is protected under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, while Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions within the circumstances specified by the Constitution.

The question, therefore, is not simply whether hospitals can regulate photography and videography.

They may need to.

The more important question is whether restrictions are specific, necessary and proportionate to the problem they seek to address.

A restriction on filming in a sensitive treatment area to protect identifiable patients is fundamentally different from a blanket rule that prevents an individual from documenting an interaction in which that individual is directly involved.

The wording of any proposed policy matters

The request submitted by Dr Mallik expressly refers not only to journalists and influencers but also to patient attendants and politicians. It also refers to previous concerns at GB Pant Hospital and ANIIMS and to an earlier administrative order concerning unauthorised entry and alleged intimidation of doctors, staff and students through photography, videography and related activities.

Those concerns may provide legitimate grounds for stronger hospital security.

But they also make precise rules important.

A workable policy should answer basic questions:

  • What exactly constitutes "unauthorised" recording?
  • Which areas are restricted?
  • Is permission required everywhere or only in designated areas?
  • Can a person record an interaction in which they are directly involved?
  • Can evidence be preserved without publication?
  • What happens when a recording concerns alleged misconduct?
  • Who determines whether a recording violates hospital rules?
  • What safeguards prevent privacy regulations from being used to suppress legitimate documentation?

These are questions of governance, not questions against the government.

Privacy and accountability need not be opposites

A balanced framework is possible.

Hospitals can prohibit filming identifiable patients without appropriate consent, protect medical records and confidential consultations, restrict recording in sensitive treatment areas and prevent interference with emergency care.

At the same time, clearly defined exceptions or procedures could address legitimate documentation of matters of public interest.

Such rules should be prominently displayed so patients, attendants, journalists and visitors understand where recording is prohibited and why.

Most importantly, the policy should regulate harmful conduct rather than assume that the presence of a camera itself constitutes harmful conduct.

The Diglipur video requires independent examination

The allegations surrounding the Diglipur video should also be treated with journalistic caution.

The communication describes the video as demonstrating obstruction, violation of patient privacy and dissemination of false information. Those are the sender's allegations, not facts established by the article.

A responsible newsroom should examine the complete recording, establish its date and location, determine what actually occurred, seek the hospital administration's response, provide the person who recorded the material an opportunity to respond, and establish precisely what information is alleged to be false.

If a police complaint or other official proceeding exists, that too should be independently confirmed.

The camera is not the enemy

A camera can document an accident.

It can preserve an interaction.

It can establish what was said.

It can record the condition of a public facility.

It can protect a citizen whose account might otherwise be disputed.

And sometimes, for a person standing alone against a much larger institution, the camera may be the only independent witness they possess.

That does not create a licence to invade a patient's privacy.

It does not justify obstructing doctors.

It does not justify entering restricted areas.

It does not justify sensationalising unverified allegations.

And it certainly does not justify publishing identifiable medical information simply because it was captured.

But neither should misconduct by some individuals become a justification for treating every citizen carrying a camera as a potential offender.

The principle should be simple

Protect the patient. Protect the medical worker. Protect the integrity of emergency care. But also protect the citizen's ability to preserve evidence and the journalist's ability to investigate matters of legitimate public interest.

A balanced policy can do all of these things.

Dweep Tulika's position is therefore not that hospitals should become unrestricted filming zones. It is that privacy and accountability require carefully defined rules rather than an unnecessarily broad approach to cameras and recording.

Because when an allegation is made, one of the most dangerous situations for any society is not that someone possesses a camera.

It is that there is no independent record of what actually happened.

title: CPI(M) Calls for World-Class Sports Infrastructure in Nicobar, Highlights Cyclist David Beckham
author: Dweep Tulika
description: CPI(M) has called for world-class sports infrastructure, training, sports medicine and sustained support for athletes in Nicobar.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | August 2026

The Andaman & Nicobar unit of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) has highlighted the sporting journey of island-born cyclist David Beckham Elkatohchoongo, calling for stronger sports infrastructure and training support for young athletes in Nicobar.

In a statement, the party described Beckham as an example of sporting talent emerging from the Islands and linked his journey to the need for better facilities and sustained institutional support for athletes.

David Beckham was named after the legendary English footballer by his football-loving family. Although he initially played football, he later took up cycling and developed into a national and international-level track cyclist. He represented India at the 2022 Commonwealth Games and 2023 Asian Games, and reached the quarter-finals of the men's sprint at the Asian Games.

His achievements have also included a gold medal in the men's elite sprint at the 2025 National Games, where he represented the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

The cyclist's journey has previously drawn national attention. In 2020, Prime Minister Narendra Modi referred to him during Mann Ki Baat, highlighting his achievements in cycling and his journey from the Andaman & Nicobar Islands to the national sporting arena.

CPI(M) said that athletes from Nicobar require access to world-class sports infrastructure, modern training facilities, sports medicine and injury-treatment services, sports science and research, and sustained support to develop their potential.

The party's statement comes amid continuing discussion over the availability of advanced sporting facilities in the Islands and the challenges faced by athletes who have to travel outside the Union Territory for specialised training.

For young athletes from remote island communities, access to appropriate training infrastructure can be an important factor in progressing from grassroots competition to national and international levels.

CPI(M) Andaman & Nicobar Islands called for greater institutional investment so that emerging athletes can pursue sporting careers without being constrained by the limitations of facilities available within the Islands.

title: MeitY Extends Deadline for Stakeholder Feedback on IT Rules Amendments
author: Dweep Tulika
description: MeitY has extended the deadline for stakeholder feedback on proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, until April 29, 2026.
labels: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
html:
New Delhi, March 30, 2026:

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has invited stakeholder feedback on proposed amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, and has extended the deadline for submissions.

The draft amendments aim to strengthen compliance by intermediaries with government-issued clarifications, advisories and directions, while enhancing oversight of digital media content regulation.

Among the key proposals, the amendments seek to clarify data retention obligations under existing laws and require intermediaries to follow guidelines issued by the Ministry as part of due diligence requirements under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

The proposed changes also expand the scope of Part III of the Rules, including extending oversight to news and current affairs content hosted by non-publisher users. The role of the Inter-Departmental Committee is also proposed to be strengthened for improved monitoring.

The Ministry stated that the amendments are intended to improve legal clarity and ensure more effective regulation of intermediary-hosted content.

Initially, stakeholders were asked to submit comments by April 14, 2026. However, following requests from various stakeholders, the Ministry extended the deadline to April 29, 2026 to allow wider participation in the consultation process.

title: Influenza Cases Largely Underreported in Winter Deaths, Study Finds
author: Dweep Tulika
description: A new study suggests influenza-related deaths may be significantly underreported in official records during winter seasons.
html:
April 19, 2026 | Barcelona

A new population-based study presented at a global infectious diseases conference has found that influenza infections may be significantly underreported in winter mortality records, with a large gap between detected cases and those officially documented as causes of death.

The research, conducted over four influenza seasons in Spain, indicated that while the virus was identified in a notable share of winter deaths through postmortem testing, only a small fraction of these cases were reflected in official death certificates, suggesting substantial underestimation of influenza-related fatalities.

The study analysed hundreds of deaths during periods of elevated seasonal mortality and involved postmortem testing for a wide range of respiratory viruses.

Findings showed that many individuals who tested positive for influenza had not been diagnosed prior to death, and a considerable proportion had not been hospitalised, pointing to missed detection in both community and clinical settings.

Researchers noted that deaths occurring outside healthcare facilities and the sudden progression of respiratory infections may contribute to the gap in diagnosis.

The analysis also highlighted that in older individuals and those with pre-existing health conditions, symptoms of influenza can be less distinct or overshadowed by chronic illnesses, leading to underlying conditions being recorded as the primary cause of death.

As a result, the role of respiratory infections in triggering deterioration may go unrecognised in official records.

The findings suggest that influenza could play a more significant role in seasonal mortality than current surveillance systems capture, prompting calls for a reassessment of monitoring approaches.

Researchers emphasised the need for broader strategies that account for deaths occurring beyond hospital settings, particularly among high-risk populations, to better understand the true impact of respiratory viral infections.

title: CM Dhami Halts Tree Felling Near Rishikesh After Week-Long Protests
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Uttarakhand CM Pushkar Singh Dhami suspends tree felling for the Bhaniyawala–Rishikesh road project after sustained environmental protests.
html:
DEHRADUN, July 24: 

Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami has ordered an immediate halt to the felling of trees for the proposed Bhaniyawala–Rishikesh road widening project following nearly a week of sustained public protests.

The controversy began on July 12 when authorities started cutting trees for the expansion of the 20-kilometre road connecting Dehradun and Rishikesh. The project requires the removal of around 4,369 trees, many located in a forest area that forms part of an important elephant corridor near Rajaji National Park. 

The move sparked widespread opposition from environmentalists, students, local residents, and social organisations. Protesters staged Chipko-style demonstrations by hugging trees, organising peaceful sit-ins, and demanding that the government reconsider the project in view of its environmental impact. Around 400 trees were reportedly felled before the work was stopped.

On July 18, Chief Minister Dhami directed officials to suspend all tree-felling activities and instructed the Chief Secretary to hold consultations with environmental experts, local communities, and other stakeholders before taking any further decision. He stated that development, environmental conservation, and public sentiment must be given equal importance. 

Meanwhile, the project's statutory clearances remain in place, while the state government's order suspending tree felling will continue until the consultation process is completed. 

The protests have drawn national attention, with many comparing them to the historic Chipko Movement, highlighting the continuing debate over balancing infrastructure development with environmental protection.

title: PM Modi’s Tricolour Pocket Squares Draw Attention on Independence Day
author: Dweep Tulika
description: PM Modi’s tricolour-themed pocket squares drew attention on Independence Day after their colour sequence sparked political and social media debate.
html:
New Delhi | August 15, 2026

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s attire during the 80th Independence Day celebrations at the Red Fort drew attention on Saturday after the tricolour-themed pocket square on his jacket appeared in a colour sequence different from that of the Indian National Flag.

The pocket square featured green, white and saffron sections, while the Indian National Flag is officially arranged with India saffron at the top, white in the middle and India green at the bottom, with the Ashoka Chakra in the centre.

The unusual colour arrangement quickly became a subject of discussion on social media and drew political reactions. Congress leaders took a swipe at the Prime Minister, pointing out that the green-white-saffron combination resembles the colour sequence of the Irish flag rather than India's saffron-white-green Tricolour.

The issue has also prompted debate over whether the pocket square should simply be viewed as a tricolour-inspired fashion accessory or whether the reversed sequence carries any significance.

The item does not appear to be a conventional Indian National Flag, and therefore describing it outright as an “upside-down national flag” could be misleading.

The Flag Code of India specifies the prescribed arrangement of the National Flag and lays down rules governing its display.

The sartorial detail came as Prime Minister Modi delivered his 13th consecutive Independence Day address from the Red Fort, continuing his tradition of wearing distinctive traditional headgear for the national occasion. This year, he wore a red Bandhani-style turban along with a white kurta and brown sleeveless jacket.

While the Prime Minister's broader Independence Day message focused on the country's development and national priorities, it was the small detail in his jacket pocket that unexpectedly became one of the day's talking points.

A Truthful & Unbiased Perspective

title: Schoolchildren in Uttar Pradesh's Fatehpur Protest Over Basic Facilities, Allege Teacher Misconduct
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Schoolchildren in Uttar Pradesh's Fatehpur protested over poor infrastructure and alleged teacher misconduct. Authorities have initiated an inquiry.
html:
Fatehpur, Uttar Pradesh | 29 July 2026

Students of a government school in Fatehpur district, Uttar Pradesh, staged a protest demanding better basic facilities, drawing attention to issues they said were affecting their learning environment.

The schoolchildren sought functioning ceiling fans, proper classroom benches, repairs to damaged classrooms and access to clean RO drinking water. Videos of the demonstration, showing students gathered outside the school premises, circulated widely on social media.

During the protest, some students also alleged that they had faced physical and verbal abuse by teachers. These allegations have not been independently verified.

Local education authorities have taken cognisance of the incident and initiated an inquiry into both the infrastructure-related complaints and the allegations made by the students. Officials have stated that appropriate action will be taken based on the findings of the investigation.

The incident has renewed attention on the quality of infrastructure in government schools and the importance of ensuring safe and supportive learning environments for children. Education experts note that access to basic facilities such as adequate seating, ventilation and clean drinking water is essential for effective learning and student well-being.

Independent verification of the students' allegations against teachers could not be established at the time of publication.

title: Iran Calls West Asia Ceasefire Deal a ‘Declaration of U.S. Defeat’
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Iran says the West Asia ceasefire agreement reflects a U.S. defeat, while Washington says the deal aims to restore regional stability.
html:
Iran Calls Ceasefire Agreement a Declaration of U.S. Defeat
Iran has described the recently brokered West Asia ceasefire agreement as a “declaration of U.S. defeat,” while Washington maintains the deal was intended to prevent further escalation and restore regional stability.

Tehran, June 24:

Iran has described the recently announced agreement aimed at ending the conflict in West Asia as a "declaration of U.S. defeat," claiming that continued resistance by regional forces compelled Washington and its allies to accept an outcome different from their original objectives.

Iranian officials said the ceasefire and diplomatic understanding marked a shift in the regional balance of power and demonstrated that military pressure had failed to achieve the goals pursued by the United States and its partners.

The remarks came after international mediation efforts resulted in an agreement intended to halt hostilities and reduce tensions across the region.

While several countries have welcomed the ceasefire as an important step towards peace and stability, Iranian leaders portrayed the agreement as evidence that their strategic position had been strengthened.

The United States and its allies have rejected that interpretation, maintaining that the primary objective of the diplomatic initiative was to prevent further escalation, protect regional security and create conditions for sustained negotiations.

Analysts say the contrasting narratives reflect the continuing geopolitical rivalry in West Asia, where both sides are attempting to shape public perception of the outcome.

Although the ceasefire has raised hopes for reducing violence, experts caution that its long-term success will depend on continued dialogue, mutual restraint and adherence to the agreed terms.

The international community has urged all parties to respect the agreement and work towards a comprehensive and lasting peace in the region.

title: NCERT Stops Distribution of Class 8 Social Science Textbook Over Content Issue
author: Dweep Tulika
description: NCERT has halted distribution of a Class 8 Social Science textbook after identifying inappropriate content in a chapter.
html:
New Delhi, 25 February 2026:

The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) has temporarily halted the distribution of its newly released Class 8 Social Science textbook after identifying inappropriate content in one of its chapters.

According to an official statement, the textbook titled “Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Vol II” was released on February 24, 2026. During review, certain inappropriate material and errors of judgment were reportedly found in Chapter 4, titled “The Role of Judiciary in our Society.”

Following the development, the Ministry of Education directed that distribution of the textbook be placed on hold until further orders.

NCERT clarified that the inclusion of the content was unintentional and reaffirmed its respect for the judiciary, describing it as a protector of the Constitution and Fundamental Rights.

The council further stated that the chapter would be revised in consultation with relevant authorities, and a corrected version of the textbook would be issued for the academic session 2026–27.

Expressing regret over the incident, NCERT apologized for the lapse and reiterated its commitment to maintaining educational standards and institutional integrity.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume VIII, Issue No. 12, dated 20 March 2026.

The meeting comes as specialised healthcare access and mainland medical referrals remain important concerns for residents of the geographically isolated Union Territory.

title: When the State Knows Where You Are, But Not Who You Are
author: Dweep Tulika
description: A political satire on the unequal efficiency of government systems: finding citizens for compliance versus responding when citizens seek services and
html:
There is a simple question hidden inside a powerful piece of political satire:

How efficiently can the state find an ordinary citizen when it wants something from them—and how efficiently can it find that same citizen when the citizen wants something from the state?

The difference can sometimes be striking.

When it comes to collecting taxes, the system knows where you live. When an instalment is overdue, reminders arrive. When a traffic violation is recorded, the challan can reach your phone. When a government fee, penalty or licence payment is due, the machinery of administration can often identify the person responsible.

In other words, when compliance is required, the citizen is rarely invisible.

But democracy demands something more than compliance.

A citizen is not merely a taxpayer, vehicle owner, consumer or beneficiary of government schemes. A citizen is also a voter, a participant in public life and a person with constitutional rights.

That is where the cartoon's final question becomes uncomfortable:

“Who are you, sir?”

The satire exposes a larger contradiction. Modern governments increasingly possess enormous amounts of information about their citizens. Digital records, identification systems, tax databases, vehicle registrations and other administrative databases have made it easier than ever to locate and identify people.

That administrative capacity is useful. It can make government services faster, reduce fraud and improve enforcement.

But efficiency should not be one-sided.

If the state can identify a citizen quickly when collecting revenue or enforcing a rule, citizens are entitled to expect comparable efficiency when they seek public services, raise grievances, demand accountability or participate in elections.

The issue, therefore, is not whether governments should know their citizens. They necessarily must, within the law and with appropriate safeguards.

The real question is:

What does the state do with that knowledge?

A government that can send a fine to a person's mobile phone should also strive to ensure that the person's legitimate complaint does not disappear into a department.

A system capable of identifying a taxpayer should be capable of providing clear information about how public money is being spent.

An administration that expects citizens to follow rules should also make it easy for citizens to understand their rights and hold institutions accountable.

The relationship between citizen and state cannot be reduced to:

“Pay, obey and move on.”

Democracy works on a two-way relationship.

Citizens have responsibilities: paying legitimate taxes, following laws and participating constructively in public life.

The state has responsibilities too: providing services, protecting rights, maintaining transparency and remaining accountable to the people it governs.

That is why the cartoon works so well.

Its humour comes from an uncomfortable possibility:

Perhaps the citizen is easiest to recognize when the state needs something from them.

The challenge for modern governance is to ensure that the citizen remains equally visible when the citizen needs something from the state.

Because a citizen should never be merely a number in a database, a taxpayer in a ledger or a challan waiting to be paid.

The same person the government can find when it wants compliance must also be seen when they ask for accountability.

That is not a favour.

That is the basic promise of democratic governance.

Dweep Tulika | A Truthful & Unbiased Perspective

title: Dr. Ratan Chandra Kar: The Doctor Who Earned the Trust of the Jarawas
author: Dweep Tulika
description: The story of Dr. Ratan Chandra Kar, who provided healthcare to the Jarawa community during the 1999 measles outbreak and later received the Padma Shri
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | August 24, 2026

When the Jarawa community of the Andaman Islands faced a serious measles outbreak in the late 1990s, one government doctor stepped into an extraordinarily difficult situation. Dr. Ratan Chandra Kar, later popularly known as the “Jarawa Doctor,” played an important role in providing medical care to the community while gradually earning its trust.

Dr. Kar arrived in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in 1998 and was posted at Kadamtala, in an area close to Jarawa territory. At the time, contact with the highly protected indigenous community was extremely limited. His work therefore involved not only treating illness but also developing a relationship of trust.

Fighting the Measles Outbreak

The most critical period came during the 1999 measles outbreak. According to a published account of his work, Dr. Kar treated more than 100 Jarawa patients during the epidemic. Many were brought to the nearby hospital for treatment and recovered.

His work was particularly important because infectious diseases can pose a serious threat to isolated indigenous populations, whose previous exposure to certain infections may be limited.

Building Trust Before Providing Treatment

Dr. Kar's contribution was not limited to prescribing medicines. He spent considerable time understanding the Jarawas and their way of life. Reports say that he learned their language and gradually developed enough trust to communicate with them.

He also travelled into remote areas to provide medical assistance rather than expecting the community to always come to a hospital. Even after his transfer to Port Blair in 2003, he continued visiting Jarawa areas to provide healthcare.

Respect for Traditional Practices

Another important aspect of his approach was his reported respect for traditional Jarawa knowledge and practices. Rather than attempting to completely replace their traditional methods, he sought to use modern medical treatment where necessary while respecting their culture.

This approach was significant because healthcare for particularly vulnerable indigenous communities requires sensitivity. Medical intervention cannot be separated from questions of culture, trust and the community's right to maintain its way of life.

Beyond the Epidemic

Dr. Kar's involvement with the Jarawas continued beyond the measles outbreak. In 2006, he became Deputy Director (Tribal and Welfare) in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands Administration, giving him a wider role in matters concerning tribal welfare.

His experience also contributed to wider understanding of the challenges involved in providing healthcare to the Jarawa community.

Padma Shri Recognition

The Government of India honoured Dr. Ratan Chandra Kar with the Padma Shri in 2023 in the field of Medicine. The official Padma Awards notification lists him among the awardees from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

His story is therefore not simply about a doctor treating an epidemic. It represents an unusual chapter in the history of healthcare in the Andaman Islands—where medical service required patience, cultural sensitivity and the ability to build trust with a community that had historically maintained limited contact with the outside world.

Dr. Kar's work remains associated with one of the significant public-health episodes involving the Jarawas and has earned him a lasting place in the medical history of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

Dweep Tulika | A Truthful & Unbiased Perspective

title: Emergency Helpline Services Restored: Numbers 100 and 112 Resume Normal Operations in Andaman & Nicobar Islands
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Andaman & Nicobar Police have restored ERSS-112 services. Emergency numbers 100 and 112 are now fully operational.
html:
The Andaman & Nicobar Police have informed the public that the technical issues affecting the Emergency Response Support System (ERSS-112) have been successfully resolved and emergency helpline services have resumed normal operations.

According to a public advisory issued by the police, emergency numbers 100 and 112 are now fully functional and available for public use.

The advisory stated that residents can once again contact the emergency helpline numbers in the event of any emergency requiring immediate police assistance.

The police also expressed appreciation for the cooperation and understanding shown by members of the public during the temporary disruption of services.

Earlier, emergency numbers 100 and 112 had experienced technical difficulties, prompting the police department to issue alternative contact numbers for emergency assistance until the issue could be resolved.

With services now restored, the public has been advised to use the standard emergency helpline numbers for assistance.

The advisory was issued in the interest of public safety by the Andaman & Nicobar Police.

title: Andaman Youth Shiyad Secures AIR 743 in UPSC Civil Services Examination 2025

Port Blair, 20 March 2026:

In a proud moment for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Shiyad has secured All India Rank (AIR) 743 in the UPSC Civil Services Examination 2025.

His achievement marks a significant milestone for the islands and highlights how determination, consistency, and perseverance can overcome geographical challenges.

Sharing his journey through a video message, Shiyad expressed gratitude towards his mentors and coaching institute for supporting him throughout his preparation process.
