title: NEET Protest Escalates After Sonam Wangchuk's Detention; Nationwide Unrest Intensifies
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Nationwide NEET protests intensified after Sonam Wangchuk's detention as students demanded examination reforms and accountability.
html:
NEW DELHI, July 21: 

The nationwide movement over the alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leak has intensified following the forcible removal and hospitalization of activist Sonam Wangchuk from his hunger strike at Jantar Mantar. What began as a protest over examination irregularities has evolved into a wider youth movement demanding accountability, examination reforms, and political responsibility.

On July 20, thousands of students attempted a "Sansad Chalo" march towards Parliament. Delhi Police stopped the procession using barricades, lathi-charge, and tear gas, resulting in violent clashes. According to reports, nearly 180 people, including protesters and police personnel, were injured, with several suffering serious injuries and undergoing treatment. As of the time of filing this report, no deaths during the protest have been officially confirmed, while authorities continue to assess the full extent of the casualties.

The protesters are demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, a transparent investigation into the alleged paper leak, accountability from the National Testing Agency (NTA), compensation for affected students and their families, and comprehensive reforms to India's examination system. Some protest groups have also expanded their demands to include the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The police action has drawn criticism from several opposition leaders and Members of Parliament, who condemned the use of tear gas and force against the demonstrators. Parliament has witnessed repeated disruptions over the issue, with opposition parties raising concerns over both the alleged examination irregularities and the handling of the protests.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has described examination paper leaks as a "grave sin" and assured strict action against those responsible while promising a stronger and more secure examination system.

Across social media, several claims about the crackdown have gone viral. These include allegations that some plain clothed individuals assaulted protesters, that several BJP workers resigned in protest, and calls to observe July 20 as a "Black Day" for Indian democracy. Social media users have also claimed that equipment beyond standard crowd-control gear including alleged 12-bore shotgun cartridges and expired tear gas shells was used or recovered during the police action. Many videos and images shared online have amplified these claims. However, none of these allegations have been independently verified or officially confirmed till now.

Protest organisers have vowed to continue demonstrations across the country until their demands are addressed. With the movement spreading to multiple states, the political and public response continues to grow.

More official details are awaited as the situation develops.

title: Santosh Pandit: The Civic Activist Who Turned Potholes Into a Public Question and Landed in Jail
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Pune civic activist Santosh Pandit is in judicial custody over alleged objectionable online content. Here is his civic activism, arrest and the questi
html:
From exposing broken roads and civic failures to facing criminal allegations over social-media posts, Pandit's arrest has raised questions about free expression, police procedure and the limits of online criticism

Pune: For years, Santosh Gajanan Pandit built his public identity around a deceptively simple idea: point a camera at problems that citizens had learned to live with.

A pothole. A damaged road. A broken drain. An alleged traffic violation. A civic project he believed had been poorly executed.

Pandit recorded them, confronted officials and public representatives, posted the encounters online and, in some cases, returned repeatedly until the issue received attention.

His approach turned ordinary civic complaints into highly visible social-media content.

Now, the 48-year-old Pune activist and content creator is in judicial custody in connection with cases concerning allegedly obscene, sexually suggestive, abusive and defamatory content posted online. A Pune court remanded him to 14 days' judicial custody on September 8 after his initial five-day police custody ended.

His arrest has generated a broader debate in Maharashtra: where does aggressive civic criticism end and allegedly criminal speech begin—and how should the police respond when that line is crossed?

The question is particularly significant because Pandit's public profile did not begin with conventional political activism.

It began with potholes.

From potholes to political scrutiny

Pandit's civic activism began attracting significant attention in 2023.

A June 2023 Hindustan Times report described him as a Pune civic influencer whose short videos focused largely on potholes, damaged roads and other municipal problems.

His methods were unconventional.

He sometimes decorated potholes with rangoli and garlands, stood beside damaged infrastructure, raised slogans and recorded the entire episode.

The strategy attracted an audience.

According to the 2023 Hindustan Times report, Pandit said his videos had contributed to the repair of more than 80 potholes. At that time, he had around 1.59 lakh YouTube followers and 16,000 Instagram followers, while one video concerning a pothole on Karve Road had crossed 19 million views.

The significance of the model was straightforward.

Pandit was not merely filing a civic complaint.

He was turning the complaint into public visibility.

And visibility can change the relationship between an ordinary citizen and a government department.

Citizens began approaching him with grievances, according to accounts of his work.

His social-media platform effectively became an informal channel through which civic problems could be amplified.

The camera became the complaint

Pandit's style was never that of a conventional civic campaigner.

Instead of simply filing a complaint and waiting for a response, he often went to the location, showed the problem on camera and directly questioned officials or public representatives.

Recent reporting has documented his videos involving civic infrastructure, traffic violations and alleged VIP treatment.

In one widely circulated episode, he confronted BJP MLA Gopichand Padalkar over an allegedly non-compliant high-security registration plate and other alleged traffic-rule violations. The encounter was recorded and circulated online.

The video reportedly attracted millions of views.

That was the power of Pandit's method.

He possessed something an ordinary complainant rarely has:

an audience.

But an audience also changes the consequences of confrontation.

As Pandit's reach expanded, his videos increasingly moved beyond potholes and municipal failures and into criticism of politicians, government decisions and alleged misuse of public authority.

The road from civic activism to confrontation

In the period immediately preceding his arrest, Pandit posted videos critical of Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, the BJP government, minister Chandrakant Patil, development projects and local civic issues, according to recent reporting.

The Padalkar confrontation became another prominent episode.

But the chronology needs careful handling.

Pandit confronted Padalkar shortly before his arrest, and the encounter was widely circulated. However, there is no established evidence that the confrontation itself was the reason for his arrest.

Police have attributed the arrest to complaints concerning allegedly objectionable content.

That distinction matters.

The midnight arrest

Pandit was arrested from his Pune residence in the early hours of September 3, 2026.

Reports differ slightly on the precise time, with police-related accounts putting it around 1 a.m. and his lawyer telling The Wire that he was picked up at approximately 12:30 a.m.

The Kothrud case followed a complaint by Sarika Ram Kamble, a Pune Municipal Corporation conservancy worker.

According to the complaint, Pandit had uploaded videos and posts containing allegedly obscene and sexually suggestive remarks concerning Maharashtra Higher and Technical Education Minister Chandrakant Patil and a woman corporator.

The reported FIR invokes Sections 75(1)(iv), 75(3), 356(2) and 352 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with Section 67 of the Information Technology Act.

The allegations include sexual harassment-related conduct, defamation, intentional insult and publication/transmission of allegedly obscene material online.

These remain allegations in an ongoing criminal case, not findings of guilt.

There was also an earlier case involving allegations concerning remarks against Chandrakant Patil, reportedly arising from a complaint by BJP corporator Sunil Pande.

That distinction is important because the two complaints should not be presented as though they were a single complaint.

Why the timing became controversial

The controversy surrounding Pandit's arrest is not limited to the allegations contained in the FIR.

It also concerns the timing and manner of the police action.

Pandit had increasingly become a visible critic of people in power. He had also publicly claimed that he was receiving threats after some of his political criticism.

The Wire reported that, shortly before his arrest, Pandit posted an audio clip in which an unidentified man allegedly abused him. Pandit claimed that the caller was associated with the BJP. That allegation has not been independently established.

Opposition politicians subsequently questioned whether the police response was proportionate and whether Pandit should have been served notice before being arrested.

NCP (Sharad Pawar) spokesperson Anish Gawande criticised the midnight arrest and invoked procedural safeguards. Maharashtra Congress chief Harshvardhan Sapkal also accused the government of intimidating critics. These are political allegations, not judicial findings.

Police, meanwhile, have maintained that the action was based on complaints and objectionable content posted online.

That leaves two questions which should be examined separately.

Was the content allegedly published by Pandit capable of constituting an offence?

That is a matter for investigation and, ultimately, the courts.

Was the timing and manner of his arrest necessary and proportionate?

That is a separate question concerning police procedure and the treatment of an accused person.

One cannot automatically answer the second question by answering the first.

From police custody to judicial custody

Pandit was initially placed in police custody.

After five days, he was produced before a Pune court on September 8, which remanded him to 14 days of judicial custody. The remand was reported to run until September 21.

Investigators have also seized the iPhone allegedly used to record the disputed reel, its SIM card and a tripod stand as part of the investigation.

The case therefore remains under investigation.

His arrest cannot be treated as proof of guilt.

But his status as a civic activist cannot, by itself, place his speech outside the reach of criminal law either.

Both principles can coexist.

Who is Santosh Pandit?

Pandit's personal history provides another layer to the story.

In a podcast interview cited by The Wire, Pandit said that he had previously operated a travel business. According to his account, the collapse in tourism following the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks badly affected the business, leaving him unable to repay loans and ultimately costing him his house and business.

This is Pandit's own account of his past and should be treated as such.

The Wire reported that Pandit started his YouTube channel in June 2022.

His earliest content was not solely about potholes. But his civic videos eventually became the defining feature of his public identity.

His formula was simple:

Find the problem. Put a camera on it. Make it difficult to ignore.

When the complaint becomes content

Pandit's rise reflects a broader change in the way citizens interact with public institutions.

Traditionally, a citizen encountering a broken road might:

  • call the municipal office;
  • submit a written complaint;
  • use a grievance portal;
  • approach an elected representative; or
  • simply live with the problem.

Pandit's approach was different.

He transformed the complaint into content.

The pothole became a visual spectacle.

The broken infrastructure became a story.

The unanswered complaint became a confrontation.

And the confrontation became something that could be viewed by hundreds of thousands—or millions—of people.

That model can be powerful.

It can also be confrontational.

And when criticism moves from documenting public failures to allegations, personal attacks, sexually coloured language or potentially defamatory statements, the legal questions become considerably more complicated.

The larger democratic question

The Santosh Pandit case is therefore larger than one influencer or one minister.

Across Indian cities, citizens routinely complain about:

broken roads, overflowing drains, traffic violations, poor infrastructure and administrative inaction.

Most complaints never become national or even citywide conversations.

Pandit's method made them visible.

That helps explain both his popularity and the controversy surrounding his style.

A functioning democracy must leave room for uncomfortable criticism of public authorities.

At the same time, criticism is not an unlimited licence for allegedly obscene, sexually harassing, threatening or defamatory speech.

The difficult task is determining where that line lies—and ensuring that the law is applied consistently, fairly and according to due process.

The questions that remain

Several questions deserve scrutiny as the case progresses:

1. What exactly did the disputed videos contain?

The full context, wording and manner in which the statements were made will matter.

2. Were the allegations against Pandit independently supported by evidence?

That is for the investigation and courts to determine.

3. What was the precise legal basis for the arrest at the time it was made?

The FIR and subsequent court proceedings will provide greater clarity.

4. Were procedural safeguards followed?

Opposition leaders and Pandit's lawyer have questioned the timing and manner of the arrest. Police have defended the action as complaint-driven.

5. Was the Padalkar confrontation connected to the arrest?

At present, the chronology alone does not establish such a connection. Police have attributed the arrest to the cases concerning allegedly objectionable online content.

6. Were complaints made by Pandit or other citizens about civic failures investigated with comparable urgency?

That is a legitimate public-accountability question—but it requires documentary evidence rather than political assertion.

The camera has turned around

Santosh Pandit became known in Pune not because he was a conventional politician.

He became known because he pointed a camera at potholes, broken infrastructure and alleged rule violations and demanded answers.

His method demonstrated the power of social media to turn an ordinary civic complaint into a public issue.

Now, following his arrest, the same camera has effectively turned in the opposite direction.

The questions are no longer only about the pothole.

They are about speech, policing, procedure, political criticism and the limits of citizen activism in the digital age.

Those questions cannot be settled by either Pandit's supporters or his critics.

They require the FIRs, the disputed videos, the police records, the court proceedings and, ultimately, judicial scrutiny.

For now, the central fact is straightforward:

Santosh Pandit is an accused in an ongoing criminal case—not a convicted offender.

And the state's response to his speech is now itself a matter of public scrutiny.

This report distinguishes between established facts, allegations made by complainants, police claims, statements attributed to Pandit and political/opposition allegations. None of the criminal allegations against Pandit should be treated as established guilt unless determined by a competent court.

title: China Calls for Faster Revival of India-China Dialogue Mechanisms
author: Dweep Tulika
description: China has urged India to accelerate the revival of suspended bilateral dialogue mechanisms during talks between Wang Yi and Ajit Doval.
html:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has urged India and China to accelerate the resumption of suspended bilateral dialogue mechanisms as both countries continue efforts to stabilize relations after years of border tensions.

New Delhi, June 23:

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has called on India and China to speed up the resumption of several bilateral dialogue mechanisms that had remained suspended following years of border tensions.

The remarks were made during a meeting with National Security Adviser Ajit Doval on the sidelines of the BRICS National Security Advisers' Meeting.

According to Chinese officials, Wang emphasized the need to strengthen communication, expand cooperation and restore regular exchanges across multiple sectors. He said both countries should work together to accelerate the revival of dialogue platforms that had been paused in recent years.

During the meeting, the two sides reviewed recent developments in bilateral relations and acknowledged the gradual progress made towards normalising ties. They also exchanged views on regional and international issues of mutual interest.

Officials said both countries reaffirmed the importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), while continuing diplomatic engagement to address differences through dialogue.

The discussions come as India and China continue efforts to rebuild trust following the prolonged military standoff along the eastern Ladakh border that began in 2020.

Observers believe that restoring regular diplomatic, economic and security dialogue mechanisms could help improve communication, reduce misunderstandings and contribute to greater stability in India-China relations.

While challenges remain, the latest meeting signals continued engagement between the two Asian neighbours as they seek to gradually normalise bilateral ties.

title: AI-Powered Mobile Operation Centres: A New Era in Policing Brings Both Promise and Concerns
author: Dweep Tulika
description: AI-powered Mobile Operation Centres are transforming policing with real-time surveillance while raising concerns over privacy, accountability and civi
html:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the way law enforcement agencies operate across the world. From predictive policing to facial recognition and drone surveillance, technology is becoming an integral part of modern policing. Among the latest innovations are AI-powered Mobile Operation Centres (MOCs) advanced command vehicles equipped with real-time surveillance systems, AI-powered analytics, facial recognition, drones, and secure communication networks.

These mobile command units are designed to improve public safety by enabling faster decision-making and better coordination during emergencies, public gatherings, disaster response and law enforcement operations. While the technology offers significant advantages, it has also sparked an important debate over privacy, accountability and the responsible use of artificial intelligence.

Enhancing Public Safety Through Technology

One of the biggest strengths of AI-powered Mobile Operation Centres is their ability to provide real-time situational awareness. Officers can monitor multiple CCTV feeds simultaneously, analyse drone footage, coordinate field personnel and respond to incidents much faster than conventional control rooms.

Artificial intelligence can automatically identify unusual crowd behaviour, detect abandoned objects, recognise missing persons and alert officers to individuals wanted in connection with serious crimes. This reduces the burden on police personnel and allows them to focus on genuine threats rather than manually monitoring hundreds of video feeds.

These systems are particularly valuable during large public events, festivals, disasters and emergency situations where rapid coordination between different agencies is essential.

AI Glasses: Bringing Information to Officers Instantly

An emerging feature of modern policing is the use of AI-enabled smart glasses. These wearable devices allow officers to receive real-time information while remaining hands-free.

Integrated with facial recognition, live databases and command centres, AI glasses can help identify wanted suspects, locate missing persons, display navigation information and provide instant alerts without requiring officers to constantly check handheld devices.

When used responsibly and within legal frameworks, AI glasses can significantly improve situational awareness and operational efficiency.

Faster Response During Emergencies

Mobile Operation Centres are also proving valuable during natural disasters, major accidents and rescue operations.

Since these units function as fully equipped mobile command posts, they can continue operating even if conventional communication infrastructure is disrupted. Live mapping, satellite communication, drone feeds and AI-assisted analytics help emergency responders make informed decisions in real time.

The ability to establish a command centre close to the affected area can substantially reduce response times and improve coordination between police, fire services, disaster management authorities and medical teams.

The Growing Privacy Debate

Despite these benefits, civil liberties experts have raised concerns about the widespread deployment of AI-powered surveillance technologies.

Continuous monitoring of public spaces may create the perception that citizens are being watched at all times. Such concerns become particularly significant during peaceful public gatherings and demonstrations, where individuals may fear that their movements or identities are being recorded and stored.

Another issue is the accuracy of facial recognition systems. While AI has improved considerably, no system is entirely error-free. Incorrect identification could lead to unnecessary questioning, detention or reputational harm for innocent individuals.

Risks of Misuse

Experts also caution that surveillance technologies must not be used beyond legitimate law enforcement purposes.

Without robust legal safeguards, independent oversight and transparent policies, there is a risk that such systems could be misused to monitor journalists, activists, political opponents or ordinary citizens.

Cybersecurity presents another challenge. Unauthorized access to surveillance networks could expose sensitive information or compromise ongoing investigations, making strong data protection measures essential.

The Need for Responsible Governance

The debate surrounding AI-powered policing is not about rejecting technology but ensuring that it is governed responsibly.

Many legal and technology experts recommend that AI surveillance should operate within a clear legal framework supported by judicial oversight, independent audits, transparency regarding data collection and retention, and accessible grievance mechanisms for citizens who believe they have been wrongly identified.

Public trust is likely to remain the most important factor in determining the long-term success of AI-enabled policing.

Finding the Right Balance

Technology has the potential to make policing smarter, faster and more effective. AI-powered Mobile Operation Centres, AI glasses, drones and intelligent surveillance systems can strengthen public safety and improve emergency response when deployed responsibly.

At the same time, protecting privacy, ensuring accountability and safeguarding fundamental rights must remain central to their implementation.

As artificial intelligence becomes an increasingly important part of law enforcement, the real challenge will not be whether society adopts these technologies, but how responsibly they are governed. The future of smart policing will ultimately depend on striking the right balance between innovation, security and individual freedoms.

title: ISRO Shifts Routine Rocket Production to Industry, Continues Launch Vehicle Development
author: Dweep Tulika
description: ISRO is shifting routine production of proven launch vehicles to Indian industry while continuing advanced rocket development and future space program
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | August 23, 2026

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is gradually shifting the routine production of established launch vehicles to Indian industry, while continuing to lead the development of new launch systems, advanced technologies and future space missions.

The change does not mean that ISRO is abandoning launch-vehicle development or stopping work on rockets. Instead, the organisation is increasingly focusing on research and development, advanced technologies, mission design and future space programmes, while established vehicles are increasingly being produced through Indian companies and industry partnerships.

The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is among the launch vehicles moving towards industry-led production. NewSpace India Limited (NSIL) has taken steps to facilitate such production, including arrangements involving Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and Larsen & Toubro.

The Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) has similarly moved towards industry production following the transfer of its technology. The objective is to expand India's launch capacity and enable industry to undertake production at commercial scale.

A similar approach is being pursued for the heavier Launch Vehicle Mark-3 (LVM3), with plans for greater private-sector participation in its production.

At the same time, ISRO will continue to play a central role in developing new launch systems and technologies, including those required for human spaceflight and future exploration missions.

This distinction is important because the statement that “ISRO will not manufacture any launch vehicle” can be misleading if interpreted as ISRO abandoning rocket development altogether.

The more accurate description is that India is moving routine production of proven launch vehicles increasingly from ISRO-led manufacturing towards industry, while ISRO concentrates more heavily on advanced research, development and future launch technologies.

The shift forms part of India's broader effort to expand private-sector participation in the space sector and build a larger domestic launch-vehicle manufacturing ecosystem.

title: Authorities Dismiss Fuel Shortage Rumours in Swaraj Dweep as Baseless
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Authorities in Swaraj Dweep dismissed viral fuel shortage rumours, stating that fuel supply on the island remains stable.
html:
Swaraj Dweep, 08 March 2026:
Rumours regarding a fuel shortage in Swaraj Dweep recently spread across social media platforms, creating concern among residents and tourists on the island.

The claims were reportedly linked to global supply concerns following tensions around the Strait of Hormuz. Videos circulating online showed long queues at petrol pumps, with several individuals alleging disruption in fuel supply and possible shortages.

However, the situation was later clarified by petrol pump authorities, who termed the rumours as misleading and baseless.

According to the branch manager, there is no shortage of fuel in Swaraj Dweep and sufficient stock is available to meet public demand.


Officials stated that the temporary rush at fuel stations was caused primarily by panic buying and minor delays in inter-island transportation, rather than any actual supply crisis.

“There is no need to panic or stock fuel. Supply is adequate, and the situation is under control,” the manager said.

Authorities have appealed to the public not to circulate unverified information on social media and advised citizens to rely only on official updates to avoid unnecessary panic.

The incident once again highlighted how misinformation online can rapidly create public concern even when the ground situation remains stable.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume VIII, Issue No. 12, dated 20 March 2026.

title: ₹48,000 Dues Pending for 4 Years: Cultural Society Moves Court in Andaman.
author: Dweep Tulika
description: A cultural society in South Andaman has moved court over pending payment dues of ₹48,000 reportedly delayed for nearly four years.
html:
Sri Vijayapuram (Port Blair), 06 Apr 26:

A registered cultural society from South Andaman has initiated legal action over non-payment of ₹48,000, pending for nearly four years despite completion and approval of assigned work.

The society, Mukta Dhara, was entrusted with two programmes in July 2022 under Ujjwala Diwas through a valid work order. According to official records, the work was completed, documents were submitted, and payment was approved. However, the amount has not been released to date.

Records indicate that the file moved across departments, including the Electricity Department in December 2023, where it was reportedly returned citing procedural issues under GFR Rule 155. The District Commissioner’s office later marked the case as “complete,” yet no final payment was made.

The society pursued multiple grievance mechanisms, including two complaints on CPGRAMS and a ministry-level representation. All were reportedly closed without resolution.

Citing prolonged delay and administrative inaction, the society issued a legal notice on 06 April 2026. The claim now includes ₹48,000 as the original amount, along with interest, compensation, and legal expenses, totaling ₹1.28 lakh.

Members of the society allege repeated follow-ups, multiple office visits, and administrative neglect during the process.

The matter has now entered the legal domain and raises broader questions regarding accountability within administrative systems, particularly in cases where work has reportedly been verified and approved but payments remain pending.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume IX, Issue No. 1.

title: New Wild Brinjal Species Discovered in Andaman Forests
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Scientists discover Solanum pandeyi, a new wild brinjal species in Middle Andaman with medicinal, genetic and agricultural potential.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram, June 22:

In a significant addition to India's botanical knowledge, scientists from the Botanical Survey of India (BSI) have discovered a new species of wild brinjal in the evergreen forests of Middle Andaman. The discovery highlights the exceptional biodiversity of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and their importance as a global ecological hotspot.

The newly identified species, named Solanum pandeyi, was discovered by Dr. Lal Ji Singh, Head of the Botanical Survey of India's Andaman and Nicobar Regional Centre. The plant was found growing naturally along forest edges in Middle Andaman and is locally known as the Wild Orange Eggplant.

According to Dr. Singh, the species has long been used by the indigenous Great Andamanese community for both food and traditional medicine. The seeds and roots are reportedly used to treat tooth infections, while the ripe fruits are prepared into a sweet-and-sour sauce using jaggery, chilli, garlic, ginger and salt by Ranchi and Bengali settler communities living on the islands.

To confirm that the plant represented a previously unknown species, researchers conducted detailed morphological and DNA-based phylogenetic analyses. The genetic study was carried out by Shruti Kasana of the University of Delhi.

The discovery has been published in the international peer-reviewed scientific journal Feddes Repertorium under the title A New Species of Solanum L. (Solanaceae) From the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, India: Taxonomic and Phylogenetic Insights.

Researchers believe the newly discovered species possesses valuable genetic traits that could assist plant breeders in developing high-yielding and disease-resistant brinjal varieties in the future. Its unique ethnobotanical importance also makes it a valuable genetic resource for scientific research.

The species has been named Solanum pandeyi in honour of Professor Arun Kumar Pandey of the Department of Botany, University of Delhi, recognising his significant contributions to plant systematics.

Dr. Singh noted that the Andaman and Nicobar Islands continue to reveal remarkable biological diversity. During the past three decades, he has documented nearly 28 plant species new to science, including wild relatives of banana and ginger, reinforcing the islands' status as one of India's richest centres of biodiversity.

The conservation status of Solanum pandeyi has currently been assessed as Data Deficient, indicating that further field surveys are required to determine its population size, distribution and long-term conservation needs.

The discovery is expected to contribute significantly to future research in botany, genetics, agriculture and biodiversity conservation while further highlighting the ecological importance of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

title: Indian Tankers Turn Back After Firing Incident in Strait of Hormuz
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Two Indian-flagged oil tankers turned back after coming under fire near the Strait of Hormuz amid rising regional tensions.
html:
Indian Tankers Turn Back After Firing Incident in Strait of Hormuz

April 19, 2026 | New Delhi

Two Indian-flagged oil tankers were forced to turn back while transiting the strategically significant Strait of Hormuz after coming under firing from Iranian gunboats amid rising regional tensions involving Iran, the United States, and Israel. 

No injuries were reported and the vessels did not sustain any damage, but the incident has heightened concerns over the safety of commercial shipping in one of the world’s most critical energy corridors, through which a substantial share of global oil and gas supplies flows. 

Communication from one of the vessels during the episode suggested confusion at sea, with crew members attempting to clarify previously granted clearance while seeking permission to withdraw from the area as the situation escalated. 

In response, India conveyed its concerns to the Iranian authorities, stressing the importance of ensuring the safety of merchant ships and seafarers and calling for the restoration of secure passage for vessels bound for Indian ports. 

The development comes amid ongoing uncertainty surrounding navigation and operational control in the strait, as evolving military and political dynamics in the region continue to disrupt maritime movement and prompt vessels to reconsider transit through the vital waterway.

The incident has once again highlighted the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz, a key global shipping route that plays a critical role in international energy security and trade.

title: NSUI Raises Concerns Over Alleged Waste Dumping Inside JNRM Campus
author: Dweep Tulika
description: NSUI raised concerns over alleged waste dumping and sanitation issues inside the JNRM college campus in Sri Vijaya Puram.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram, March 2026:

The National Students' Union of India (NSUI) has raised concerns regarding alleged negligence in waste management at Jawaharlal Nehru Rajkeeya Mahavidyalaya (JNRM), Sri Vijaya Puram.

According to Y Arvind Rao, a large quantity of garbage was reportedly found dumped near the bike parking area close to Gate No. 2 of the college campus.

He alleged that the waste had not been cleared for a considerable period and that sanitation measures were inadequate, raising concerns over hygiene and potential health risks for students.

Rao further stated that a complaint has been submitted to the Sri Vijayapuram Municipal Council (SVPMC), urging immediate intervention and clearance of the waste.

He warned that if prompt action is not taken, stronger measures may be adopted to highlight the issue publicly.

Describing the situation as an “irresponsibility of the college management,” Rao emphasized the need for proper maintenance and sanitation within educational institutions to ensure a safe and healthy environment for students.

title: Weigh Bridge, NH-4 and Higher Education: AAP’s Dr Arun Kumar Mallik Outlines Demands and Government Follow-Up
author: Dweep Tulika
description: AAP leader Dr Arun Kumar Mallik discusses weigh bridges, NH-4, road safety and higher education, including BBA in North & Middle Andaman and local gue
html:
Weigh Bridge, NH-4 and Higher Education: AAP’s Dr Arun Kumar Mallik Outlines Demands and Government Follow-Up

Port Blair: Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) Andaman & Nicobar State President Dr Arun Kumar Mallik addressed a press briefing covering two broad sets of issues concerning the islands — the operation and enforcement of weigh bridges and weight restrictions along NH-4, and a range of higher-education concerns, including the proposed private university regulation, introduction of a BBA course in North & Middle Andaman, and preference for local candidates in guest lecturer appointments.

At the outset, Dr Mallik said the briefing was intended to provide updates on issues that had recently generated public discussion, particularly the weigh bridge issue and higher education in the islands. He was accompanied by AAP Vice President Sultan Ahmed.

Weigh Bridge Issue: From Representation to Technical Examination

Dr Mallik said the issue came to his attention after members of the Andaman Nicobar Truck Owners Association approached him and requested that he take up their concerns with the Administration.

According to him, the association had been attempting since 2023 to establish a weigh bridge. He said that by the end of 2024, the facility had been constructed with specifications required for a weigh bridge on a National Highway and that it was inaugurated in 2025. However, he claimed that the facility remained non-operational for approximately a year.

Dr Mallik said he subsequently examined the available documentation and, along with another representative, inspected the weigh bridge located along NH-4 near Mayabunder. Following the inspection, he said he submitted a representation to the Andaman & Nicobar Administration's concerned Shipping and Transport authorities, requesting that the facility be operationalised.

He argued that operationalising the weigh bridge was important not simply as an enforcement measure but also from a road-safety perspective.

According to Dr Mallik, controlling vehicle weight could help prevent excessive loading, reduce damage to roads and potentially lower the risk of accidents involving drivers of overloaded vehicles.

Enforcement Begins and Surprise Checks Conducted

Dr Mallik said the Administration subsequently examined the matter and that the weigh bridge became operational after his representation.

He also credited the Regional Transport Office (RTO) with beginning surprise checks. According to his account, several vehicles were checked and penalties were imposed for violations, with enforcement being carried out in connection with the applicable rules governing NH-4.

The enforcement, however, subsequently became controversial among sections of truck owners, according to Dr Mallik.

He said some vehicle owners opposed the restrictions because vehicles that had previously been carrying loads beyond permitted limits were no longer able to do so. He also referred to a strike and a protest involving a truck/pickup association in Diglipur, while expressing his view that the protest was unnecessary.

Allegations of Selective Enforcement

Another concern raised by Dr Mallik was what he described as complaints of uneven or selective enforcement.

He said some vehicle owners were alleging that certain vehicles were being stopped or checked while others carrying excess weight were not being subjected to the same action.

He subsequently submitted another representation to the Administration, outlining what he described as four principal requests:

  • Construction of an additional weigh bridge
  • Continuation of enforcement and surprise checks
  • Making use of the existing weigh bridge mandatory for commercial goods vehicles
  • Exemptions or special arrangements for vehicles transporting perishable goods

Dr Mallik said the objective should be to ensure that commercial goods vehicles travelling between Port Blair and Diglipur through NH-4 are subject to appropriate weight checks.

The allegation of selective enforcement was presented during the briefing as a concern raised by vehicle owners; the briefing material does not independently establish whether enforcement was in fact selective.

Fresh Vegetables and Perishable Goods

One of the more specific requests concerned vehicles carrying fresh vegetables and other perishable goods.

Dr Mallik said he had received complaints that farmers and vegetable sellers in Diglipur were being affected by delays associated with the protest and restrictions.

He said he contacted a farmers' association in Diglipur and was told that vegetables were being affected.

He therefore requested that vehicles carrying perishable goods receive appropriate consideration so that essential produce could move without unnecessary delay. He also referred to exemption from the applicable user fee for such vehicles as part of his representation.

NHIDCL Examines the Proposals

A major portion of the briefing centred on a response that Dr Mallik said he had received from NHIDCL following his representation.

He said the Administration had officially forwarded his requests to NHIDCL for technical examination because the proposals related to NH infrastructure.

According to Dr Mallik, NHIDCL's engineers examined the five requests contained in his representation.

On the proposal for an additional weigh bridge, Dr Mallik said the technical response described the idea positively, while making clear that the decision to construct a new facility would have to be taken by the concerned Transport Department and Administration.

He emphasised that an additional weigh bridge could not simply be constructed immediately and would require planning, funding and coordination between departments and districts.

He said the issue could involve both North & Middle Andaman and South Andaman, requiring coordination across the relevant administrative and transport authorities.

Mandatory Use of the Existing Weigh Bridge

Dr Mallik also advocated making the existing weigh bridge mandatory for commercial goods vehicles.

His argument was that all commercial goods vehicles travelling on NH-4 between Port Blair and Diglipur should undergo weight checks to determine whether they were carrying loads within the permitted limits.

He said the technical response from NHIDCL had also addressed the issue and that implementation would require coordination among the Transport Department, Legal Metrology authorities and the district administration.

According to Dr Mallik, the objective was not merely to penalise drivers but to ensure compliance with weight restrictions and protect the road infrastructure.

12-Tonne Restriction and Ferry Safety

Another issue discussed was the 12-tonne maximum weight restriction in connection with vehicle movement through the ferry system.

Dr Mallik said the 12-tonne figure had a technical basis and referred to it as a weight limit advised in relation to ferry safety. He said vehicles exceeding the permissible weight could create a risk of damage to the ferry.

He maintained that the relevant technical recommendations should be strictly complied with.

The briefing material contains some unclear automated transcription around the precise technical terminology and the departments involved, and those portions have therefore not been expanded beyond what can reasonably be established from the recording transcript.

Road Safety at the Centre of the Argument

Dr Mallik repeatedly linked the weigh bridge issue to road safety.

He said weight control could prevent excessive loading and help preserve the road surface. He also argued that lighter and properly loaded vehicles would be easier for drivers to operate and could reduce accident risks.

He appealed to truck owners and drivers to comply with the applicable rules, noting that enforcement action can directly affect drivers even when the vehicle is owned by someone else.

He further argued that changes to enforcement practices may initially cause inconvenience but eventually become part of normal road-safety compliance.

NH-4 Progress and Future Construction

Dr Mallik also spoke about the wider development of NH-4.

He said he had met an NHIDCL Executive Director in Port Blair and discussed the challenges associated with completing the highway.

He said one of his principal concerns was the condition and connectivity of roads serving residents of North & Middle Andaman.

According to information he said was shared during the meeting, NH-4 was expected to reach significant milestones in the coming period. However, the briefing material contains some unclear dates and place names in this portion, and the specific completion dates mentioned verbally should therefore be treated as statements attributed to the speaker rather than independently verified project timelines.

Dr Mallik said he intended to continue pursuing the issue of an additional weigh bridge in his capacity as AAP State President, while acknowledging that construction would require administrative decisions, funding and inter-departmental coordination.

Higher Education: Second Major Issue

After concluding the weigh bridge and NH-4 discussion, Dr Mallik moved to the second major subject of the briefing — higher education in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

He referred to the recent controversy surrounding the introduction and transition towards the new university system and said the protests associated with the issue had subsequently been withdrawn.

He also discussed the proposed Andaman & Nicobar Private University Regulation, 2026, stressing that a regulation being formulated should not automatically be interpreted as meaning that multiple private universities had already been established in the islands.

Private University Regulation 2026

Dr Mallik said he had submitted his comments and suggestions concerning the proposed private university regulation.

He said he had spoken with the Directorate/Department of Higher Education and received information that some of the suggestions he had submitted were being considered.

He also used the issue to emphasise his approach to political engagement, saying that he communicates with officials through letters and emails and follows up on representations rather than limiting his efforts to social media posts.

He cited his correspondence on the weigh bridge issue as an example, saying that the Administration had acted on his representation by referring the matter to NHIDCL for technical examination.

Demand for BBA Course in North & Middle Andaman

Dr Mallik then raised a specific educational demand from North & Middle Andaman.

He said a resident from the region had approached him regarding the absence of a Bachelor of Business Administration (BBA) course at Mahatma Gandhi Government College.

According to him, several higher-education institutions in Port Blair already offer management-related education, but students in North & Middle Andaman do not have the same access to a BBA course locally.

Dr Mallik said introducing BBA at the college would provide students with access to management education closer to home and potentially equip them with skills that could be used in further education and employment.

He said he had received a written representation on the issue and had subsequently written to the Education Department. He added that the department was considering the proposal.

Preference for Local Candidates as Guest Lecturers

The third higher-education issue concerned the appointment of guest lecturers.

Dr Mallik said guest lecturers are appointed from both the mainland and within the islands.

He said he had received information that the Administration was considering giving first preference to eligible local PhD-qualified candidates before considering candidates from the mainland.

He welcomed such a move and argued that qualified local candidates should receive preference in guest lecturer appointments.

He connected this position with his broader advocacy for greater employment opportunities for Islanders, reiterating his stated preference for a high level of reservation of government jobs for local candidates.

Two Sets of Issues, One Broader Political Message

The press briefing ultimately brought together two very different policy areas.

On transport and infrastructure, Dr Mallik's focus was on the functioning of the weigh bridge, enforcement of vehicle weight limits, road safety, protection of NH-4, ferry-related restrictions, an additional weigh bridge and special consideration for vehicles carrying perishable goods.

On higher education, he focused on the proposed Private University Regulation 2026, the transition to the new university system, introducing BBA at Mahatma Gandhi Government College in North & Middle Andaman, and giving preference to qualified local candidates for guest lecturer positions.

A recurring theme throughout the briefing was the role of written representations and administrative follow-up.

Dr Mallik presented the technical examination by NHIDCL as an example of how a political representation can move from a public demand to examination by the relevant technical authority.

At the same time, several statements made during the briefing—including allegations regarding selective enforcement, descriptions of protests as unnecessary, and projected timelines for NH-4—remain claims or assessments made by the speaker and are not independently established by the briefing material.

The briefing concluded with Dr Mallik thanking Islanders and those watching the live broadcast for following the two sets of issues.

title: Major Decisions Taken by the C. Joseph Vijay Government Since Assuming Office
author: Dweep Tulika
description: A look at the key Cabinet decisions, welfare measures, policy initiatives and Assembly resolutions of the C. Joseph Vijay government.
html:
Chennai, June 27:

Since taking oath as Chief Minister on 10 May 2026, C. Joseph Vijay has initiated a series of administrative decisions, welfare measures and policy directions aimed at implementing the government's election commitments and strengthening public service delivery across Tamil Nadu.

During its first Cabinet meeting, the government reviewed 436 election promises and development projects, directing all departments to prepare Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) for time-bound implementation. Progress is being monitored through the Special Programme Implementation Department with an emphasis on transparency and corruption-free governance.

Among the government's flagship initiatives is the "Lady Singham" women's safety programme, aimed at strengthening women's police patrols, improving emergency response systems and ensuring faster action against crimes against women. Existing welfare programmes for women have also been continued.

In the transport sector, the government has retained free bus travel for women and continued concessional bus pass schemes for students with administrative improvements.

The administration has also prioritised improvements in government schools, expansion of student welfare measures and scholarships, strengthening of public hospitals and primary healthcare, and enhancement of preventive health programmes.

For the agriculture and fisheries sectors, the government has included welfare measures for farmers, fishermen and agricultural labourers in its implementation roadmap, alongside irrigation and rural infrastructure projects.

A statewide anti-drug campaign has also been launched, focusing on narcotics enforcement, action against illegal gutka sales and awareness programmes targeting youth and educational institutions.

Water security has emerged as another priority, with a five-year plan to provide 24×7 drinking water supply in municipal corporations while also pursuing restoration of the Cooum River and Buckingham Canal.

Following the ammonia leak incident in Tiruvallur district, the government ordered safety audits of hazardous industries and directed authorities to strengthen industrial safety protocols across the state.

Economic development remains a key focus, with initiatives to attract investment, promote industrial growth, support MSMEs and create employment opportunities.

The government has also reaffirmed its commitment to promoting Tamil language and culture, including seeking national recognition for the Thirukkural.

On Centre-State issues, the administration has reiterated its demand for exemption from NEET, release of pending Central funds and greater autonomy for Tamil Nadu on selected policy matters.

The Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly also unanimously adopted a resolution opposing Karnataka's proposed Mekedatu Dam Project, urging the Union Government not to grant clearance and seeking protection of Tamil Nadu's rights over Cauvery river waters.

The government has additionally expanded its Council of Ministers and appointed a Special Representative in New Delhi to strengthen coordination with the Central Government.

As of 27 June 2026, the administration has announced more than 10 major Cabinet and governance decisions, initiated implementation of 436 projects and welfare commitments, and adopted one major Assembly resolution while focusing on women's safety, education, healthcare, transport, drinking water, employment, agriculture, anti-drug enforcement and good governance.

title: 13 Hospitalized After STS School Bus Accident Near Kishorinagar in North Andaman
author: Dweep Tulika
description: An STS school bus carrying students skidded off the road near Kishorinagar, North Andaman. Thirteen people were hospitalized.
html:
Diglipur, July 10:

An Andaman and Nicobar State Transport Service (STS) school bus carrying students from Kishorinagar towards Talbagan met with an accident on Friday morning after reportedly skidding off the road.

According to information available from government and local sources, passengers were safely evacuated from the vehicle and shifted to the Primary Health Centre (PHC), Kishorinagar, before personnel from the Fire & Emergency Services reached the accident site.

The vehicle involved has been identified as an STS bus attached to Paschim Sagar, bearing Registration No. AN 01 G 0034, manufactured by Tata Motors Ltd.

Vehicle registration records indicate that the bus is classified as a Bus (LPV), BS-II compliant, with a seating capacity of 45 passengers. It was registered on 21 December 2012, making it approximately 14 years and 4 months old, while its certificate of fitness remains valid until 1 December 2026.

According to the latest available information, 13 persons have been hospitalized, the majority of them being school students. Officials have not yet released details regarding the severity or nature of the injuries.

Some people after the accident have alleged that the driver was under the influence of alcohol at the time of the incident. However, Dweep Tulika has not independently verified these claims. No official statement has been issued by the Police, Transport Department, or Health authorities confirming the allegation. The exact cause of the accident remains under investigation.

This is a developing story. Dweep Tulika will continue to update readers as more verified information becomes available.

title: Why Should India Wait Until 2047?
author: Dweep Tulika
description: India's 2047 development vision is ambitious, but citizens also need measurable improvements in jobs, healthcare, infrastructure and public services t
html:
A developed India cannot be a promise for tomorrow. Citizens need to experience measurable progress today.

For years, Indians have been asked to look towards the future.

2047 has become one of the country's defining development milestones — the year India aims to complete 100 years of independence as a developed nation.

There is nothing wrong with having an ambitious national goal.

The question is what happens between now and then.

An Indian citizen living in 2026 does not live in 2047.

That citizen pays taxes today. Pays GST today. Pays electricity bills, transport costs, school fees and medical expenses today.

So the legitimate question is simple:

Why should citizens have to wait until 2047 to experience the basic standards of a modern, efficient country?

The world is already moving

Technology is moving rapidly from laboratories into everyday life.

Autonomous vehicles are being deployed in some markets. Drone technology is moving towards increasingly practical commercial applications. Agricultural robotics, artificial intelligence, precision farming, electric mobility and automated logistics are developing rapidly.

India is participating in this transformation too.

The country has made significant advances in digital public infrastructure, digital payments, space technology, renewable energy and other areas.

But technological achievements at the national level are only one part of development.

The more important question for an ordinary citizen is:

Can I feel the improvement in my everyday life?

Can a patient access healthcare without excessive waiting?

Can a young person find productive and meaningful employment?

Can a farmer access modern technology without being priced out?

Can a citizen obtain a government certificate without making repeated visits to an office?

Can people depend on public transport?

Can cities provide reliable water, sanitation, waste management and roads?

Can a complaint to a government department be resolved quickly and transparently?

These are not futuristic demands.

They are basic expectations of a modern public-service system.

2047 cannot become an excuse for 2026

The World Bank's current India Country Partnership Framework for 2026–31 explicitly links the country's 2047 ambition with jobs, rural prosperity, urban transformation, human capital, infrastructure, water, waste management, digital connectivity and energy security. It also identifies the need for reforms and investment to accelerate India's development trajectory.

The World Bank has separately said that India needs faster and more inclusive growth, greater investment, stronger productivity and greater labour-force participation to reach high-income status by 2047.

That matters because becoming developed is not achieved simply by announcing a target year.

It is achieved through thousands of improvements made every year.

2047 should be the destination — not the reason today's problems are postponed.

Citizens don't need only mega-projects

India can build highways, airports, digital platforms and large infrastructure projects while citizens continue to struggle with basic services.

Both things can exist at the same time.

A country can have sophisticated digital systems while a citizen struggles to correct a simple government record.

It can discuss artificial intelligence while some schools continue to face shortages of basic resources.

It can aspire to become a global manufacturing power while young people continue asking where stable and productive jobs will come from.

It can develop smart-city infrastructure while residents continue demanding reliable water, drainage, waste collection and public transport.

This does not mean large infrastructure projects are unnecessary.

It means infrastructure and everyday public services must progress together.

The World Bank's current framework itself places livable cities, essential services, transport, water, wastewater and waste management alongside digital connectivity and emerging technologies.

That is the point often lost in the race for headline-making projects.

Development should not be measured only by what a country builds. It should also be measured by how people live.

The tax question

Citizens are not necessarily opposed to paying taxes.

People understand that governments need revenue to build infrastructure, fund welfare programmes, maintain institutions and provide public services.

The legitimate question is different:

What does the citizen receive in return?

If compliance becomes more demanding, government systems should become simpler.

If technology makes administration easier for the state, citizens should experience that convenience too.

If the economy grows, people should be able to see that growth through better opportunities, higher productivity and improved living standards.

The relationship should increasingly move away from:

Pay → wait → visit another office → submit another document → follow up again.

And towards:

Pay → access → receive → resolve.

That is the direction a modern public-service system should aspire to take.

And what about ordinary people?

India's 2047 journey cannot be measured only through investors, corporations, mega-projects or economic statistics.

The small entrepreneur matters.

The farmer matters.

The worker matters.

The student matters.

The elderly citizen matters.

The person waiting outside a government hospital matters.

The commuter spending hours travelling every day matters.

The family struggling with rising living costs matters.

The citizen who has lost confidence after repeatedly dealing with an inefficient public office matters.

A developed nation is ultimately not a photograph of a new airport.

It is the experience of its people.

Competing with the world means fixing the fundamentals

India wants to compete with the world's leading economies.

That requires technological ambition.

But it also requires reliable infrastructure, skilled workers, productive businesses, strong schools, accessible healthcare and predictable government systems.

The World Bank's current partnership framework makes a similar connection: jobs and skills, livable cities, rural prosperity, infrastructure, transport, digital connectivity, water and waste systems are all part of the development agenda supporting the 2047 vision.

These are not secondary issues.

They are the foundation.

A country cannot sustainably compete at the technological frontier if citizens and businesses spend enormous amounts of time navigating avoidable administrative problems.

Technology should reduce friction.

Government should reduce friction.

Infrastructure should reduce friction.

Economic growth should create opportunity.

That is what progress should feel like.

Don't ask citizens to wait. Show them the journey.

The answer to India's challenges is neither pessimism nor blind optimism.

It is measurement and accountability.

If 2047 is the destination, citizens should be able to ask every year:

What improved this year?

How many government services became faster?

How many schools improved?

How many hospitals became more accessible?

How many productive jobs were created?

How much did commuting improve?

How much did agricultural productivity increase?

How much did the time and cost of dealing with government decrease?

How many government processes were eliminated because technology made them unnecessary?

And most importantly:

Did the quality of life of ordinary citizens improve?

These questions should not belong exclusively to one political party.

They belong to the citizen.

India doesn't need to wait for 2047 to become better

The dream of a developed India is not the problem.

The question is what happens between today and 2047.

A country does not suddenly wake up on January 1, 2047 and become developed.

It becomes developed because every year before that, institutions become better, services become more reliable, technology becomes more accessible, jobs become more productive and citizens gain greater confidence in their institutions.

So the demand from citizens should not be:

“Give us 2047 today.”

It should be:

“Show us progress today.”

Let 2047 remain the national destination.

But let 2026 be measured by what actually improves in 2026.

Because the people of India are not merely the audience for a future vision.

They are the people paying for, working through and living through the journey.

And they have every right to ask:

If we are expected to build the India of 2047, shouldn't we be able to live a better India today?

title: Supreme Court Reaffirms SC Status Limited to Hindu, Sikh and Buddhist Communities
author: Dweep Tulika
description: The Supreme Court has reaffirmed that Scheduled Caste status remains limited to Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists under existing law.
html:
New Delhi, April 20:

The Supreme Court of India has reiterated that Scheduled Caste (SC) status is restricted to individuals professing Hinduism, Sikhism, or Buddhism, in line with the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950.

The Court clarified that a person belonging to a Scheduled Caste who converts to another religion, such as Christianity or Islam, ceases to be recognised as an SC from the moment of conversion. As a result, such individuals are no longer entitled to reservation benefits or legal protections available under laws including the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.

The ruling came while upholding a lower court decision and reaffirming the existing constitutional framework governing SC recognition. The bench
observed that the legal status of Scheduled Castes is explicitly linked to the three specified religions under the Presidential Order issued in 1950.

Originally limited to Hindus, the scope of SC recognition was extended to Sikhs in 1956 and Buddhists in 1990 through subsequent amendments. However, individuals professing other religions remain outside its ambit under the current legal framework.

The Court further noted that any change in this position would require legislative intervention and cannot be addressed through judicial interpretation alone.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume IX, Issue No. 1.

title: DISHA Meeting in South Andaman Postponed Over Non-Availability of Documents
author: Dweep Tulika
description: The DISHA meeting in South Andaman chaired by MP Bishnu Pada Ray was postponed due to lack of required documents.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram, 26 February 2026:

The DISHA (District Development Coordination and Monitoring Committee) meeting of South Andaman, chaired by Member of Parliament Bishnu Pada Ray, was postponed after a scheme-wise review could not be conducted due to the alleged non-availability of required administrative documents.

According to a statement issued by the MP’s office, effective monitoring of Central Sponsored Schemes requires complete records, transparency, and access to relevant departmental documents.

In the absence of the necessary information and documents, the scheduled review process could not proceed and the meeting was subsequently postponed.

The MP emphasized the importance of proper review mechanisms to ensure accountability, transparency, and development-oriented governance in South Andaman district.

He further expressed hope for full cooperation from the administration during the next session so that a comprehensive review of various schemes can be carried out in the interest of public welfare and district development.

Originally published in Dweep Tulika, Volume VIII, Issue No. 12, dated 20 March 2026.

title: Sugar and Edible Oil Prices Put Fresh Pressure on Household Budgets
author: Dweep Tulika
description: Sugar and edible-oil prices are putting pressure on household budgets, with consumers in Andaman and Nicobar facing additional supply-chain costs.
html:
Sri Vijaya Puram | August 23, 2026

Household grocery budgets are facing fresh pressure as prices of some essential commodities, particularly sugar and edible oils, have increased in recent weeks. However, the increase has not been uniform across all essential food items.

Sugar has emerged as one of the most notable areas of concern. Recent reports indicate that sugar prices in India have risen amid tighter supplies, prompting the Centre to take measures to improve availability, including allowing duty-free imports of raw sugar.

Edible oils have also remained expensive. Government data indicates a significant increase in edible-oil prices, while recent market reports show particularly high prices for sunflower and other cooking oils in several states.

Some pulses have recorded more moderate increases. Recent government data showed increases in the prices of urad dal, tur dal and masoor dal, while moong dal recorded a relatively smaller movement.

For consumers in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the impact of commodity prices is particularly important because transportation and supply-chain costs can make retail prices higher than mainland averages.

Government-derived data for August 14 recorded rice at around ₹55.67 per kg, sugar at ₹58.67 per kg, groundnut oil at around ₹294.50 per litre and milk at ₹74 per litre in the Islands.

However, these figures represent price levels on a particular date and should not, by themselves, be described as a monthly “hike”. A proper assessment requires comparison with earlier official prices.

The current situation therefore points to selective price pressure rather than a blanket increase across all groceries. Consumers are likely to feel the greatest impact from sugar and cooking-oil prices, while movements in other staples remain comparatively moderate.

Source: Ministry of Consumer Affairs price-monitoring data and recent market reports.
