title: AAP’s Arun Mallik Seeks BBA Course at MGGC Mayabunder from 2027–28
author: Dweep Tulika
description: AAP leader Arun Mallik urges the A&N Administration to introduce a BBA degree at MGGC Mayabunder from the 2027–28 academic session.
html:
Mallik says students from North and Middle Andaman face difficulties travelling to Port Blair to pursue BBA

03 Sep 2026, Sri Vijayapuram:
Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) Andaman & Nicobar Islands State President Dr Arun Kumar Mallik has requested the Andaman & Nicobar Administration to introduce a Bachelor of Business Administration (BBA) degree course at Mahatma Gandhi Government College (MGGC), Mayabunder, from the 2027–28 academic session.

In a letter dated 3 September 2026 addressed to the Commissioner-cum-Secretary (Education/Sports) of the A&N Administration, Mallik said the proposal was aimed particularly at students from North and Middle Andaman District who wish to pursue undergraduate studies in business administration.

BBA currently available in Port Blair institutions

Mallik said the BBA degree course is currently available at ANCOL, while Jawaharlal Nehru Rajkeeya Mahavidyalaya (JNRM) offers a BBA course in Tourism & Travel Management.

He noted that both institutions are located in Port Blair, South Andaman District. According to his letter, MGGC and the Port Blair institutions offer several similar degree courses, but BBA is not currently available at MGGC.

Mallik argued that students from North and Middle Andaman who want to pursue BBA therefore have to consider moving to or studying in Port Blair.

He said this can be particularly difficult for students from lower socio-economic backgrounds, and claimed that some students may instead opt for general BA, BSc or BCom courses available at MGGC.

Proposal aimed at expanding local higher education

Mallik described BBA as a three-year undergraduate management programme covering areas related to business, commerce and administration.

He argued that the Islands' ongoing development, including infrastructure projects, digital connectivity and eco-tourism initiatives, could create greater demand for management-related skills.

According to Mallik, introducing BBA at MGGC would provide an additional higher-education option for students in North and Middle Andaman and could benefit Islanders, particularly those who may find it difficult to pursue the course in Port Blair.

Request for consideration from 2027–28

Mallik has requested the Education Department to examine the proposal and consider introducing the BBA course at MGGC, Mayabunder, from the 2027–28 academic session.

The letter also refers to MGGC's institutional transition, stating that the college was historically affiliated with Pondicherry University and has transitioned into a constituent college of the Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose Institute of Higher Learning (NSCBIHL). Mallik copied the Vice-Chancellor of NSCBIHL on his request.

Request sent to higher education authorities

The communication was addressed to the Commissioner-cum-Secretary (Education/Sports) and copied to the Vice-Chancellor of NSCBIHL, Director of Education/Sports/Higher Education, Secretary (Education), Secretary to the Lieutenant Governor and Chief Secretary, among others.

Mallik said he and members of the AAP A&N Islands unit planned to seek a meeting with the Education Secretary to discuss the proposal further.

A proposal, not yet an approved course

The letter represents Mallik's request to the Administration. It does not establish that the BBA course has been approved at MGGC or that admissions will begin from 2027–28.

Any decision would depend on the competent authorities and the institutional process governing introduction of a new degree programme.

Editorial Note: This report is based on Dr Arun Kumar Mallik's representation dated 3 September 2026. The attached Annex 1, described in the email as a letter from another A&N Islander, is referenced in the document but its substantive contents are not reproduced in the available text.

title: ‘CA, Aerospace Engineer’ vs ‘Driver, Tourism’: Manoj Paul’s Post Sparks Debate Over Children’s Career Aspirations
author: Dweep Tulika
description: ANDC leader Manoj Paul compares career aspirations of children in Chennai and Rangat, sparking discussion on education and exposure in Andaman.
html:
09 Sep 2026, Chennai: 

A social media post by Andaman Nicobar Democratic Congress (ANDC) leader Manoj Paul has sparked discussion about educational exposure and career aspirations among children in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

In a video shared by Paul, he is seen travelling in an autorickshaw in Chennai and interacting with two young passengers. When asked about their future aspirations, one child, who says he is studying in Class 9, says he wants to become a Chartered Accountant (CA). Another child, identified in the post as Mukundan, says he wants to become an aerospace engineer.

Paul appreciates the children for having what he describes as a clear vision for their future.

The video then refers to an earlier interaction Paul says he had with a boy and a girl in Rangat, North and Middle Andaman. According to the post, the boy said he wanted to become a driver, while the girl expressed an interest in working in the hotel and tourism sector.

Paul compares career aspirations

Using the two sets of interactions, Paul argues that there is a difference in the “vision and mentality” of children depending on their geographical location and exposure.

He expresses concern that children in the Islands may not be sufficiently interested in higher education and may be more likely to consider occupations such as driving or tourism.

Paul subsequently appeals to parents in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to consider sending their children to the mainland for education. He argues that greater exposure could broaden their thinking and awareness of career opportunities.

What can individual responses tell us?

The comparison, however, also raises a broader question about whether responses from a small number of children can be used to draw conclusions about the educational aspirations of an entire community.

A child's stated career preference can be influenced by many factors, including family circumstances, personal interests, exposure, school environment and awareness of different professions.

Occupations such as driving and employment in tourism are also legitimate livelihoods and do not, by themselves, indicate a lack of ambition or interest in education.

The larger issue of educational exposure

At the same time, Paul's post draws attention to a question that warrants wider discussion: whether children in remote island communities have the same access to career counselling, professional role models, higher-education options and exposure to different career paths as children in larger mainland cities.

Rather than comparing individual career choices alone, the issue can also be examined through the factors that shape children's aspirations, including the quality and availability of schooling, access to higher education, career guidance, family circumstances, connectivity and exposure to opportunities beyond the Islands.

Paul's post has therefore opened a conversation about the relationship between educational exposure and career aspirations, while also raising questions about how the Islands can ensure that young people are aware of the broad range of educational and professional opportunities available to them.

Editorial Note: The statements regarding the children's responses and the comparison between Chennai and Rangat are based on Manoj Paul's social media video/post. The experiences of the individual children should not be treated as representative of all students or children in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

title: IndiGo Flight’s Emergency Landing Raises Safety Concerns for Frequent Flyers
author: Dweep Tulika
description: An IndiGo flight made a precautionary emergency landing after suspected engine failure, raising renewed aviation safety concerns.
html:
New Delhi/ Port Blair, 28 Mar 2026:

A recent mid-air emergency involving an IndiGo flight has brought aviation safety into sharp focus, particularly for regions heavily dependent on air connectivity like the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The aircraft, operating on the Visakhapatnam–Delhi route, was forced to make a precautionary emergency landing in the national capital after a suspected engine failure was detected during the flight.

The aircraft was carrying 161 passengers at the time of the incident. According to available information, the pilots identified the technical issue early and followed established safety procedures, declaring an emergency and diverting the flight to Delhi. The landing was executed safely, with emergency response teams on standby, and no injuries were reported.

Passengers were later deboarded without incident, highlighting the effectiveness of standard aviation safety protocols.

While such precautionary landings are part of global aviation practice, the incident has raised concerns due to the airline’s extensive role in connecting remote regions. In places like Port Blair, where air travel remains the primary link to mainland India, IndiGo operates frequent services through Veer Savarkar International Airport, making reliability and safety critical for both residents and tourists.

Aviation authorities have initiated a detailed technical inspection of the aircraft to determine the exact cause of the suspected engine malfunction. Experts note that modern aircraft are designed with multiple safety layers, allowing flights to continue or land safely even in the event of a single engine issue.

However, repeated or high-profile incidents often trigger broader discussions around maintenance standards, operational checks, and regulatory oversight.

At present, there has been no official confirmation of disruptions to IndiGo’s scheduled services, including those connecting the Andaman region. However, the incident serves as a reminder of the importance of stringent safety compliance in an industry where even minor technical lapses can have significant consequences.

As the investigation continues, aviation regulators are expected to review the findings closely. The outcome may influence future safety audits and operational protocols, especially for airlines serving critical connectivity routes across India.
